Tomorrow morning, Wednesday, October 14, 2026, the absolute parent proxy for the entire global technology sector takes the microphone. While casual retail traders spend their weeks watching day-to-day stock price swings on secondary chip designers, institutional smart money is laser-focused on the Netherlands. Tomorrow's high-stakes third-quarter financial report from ASML Holding isn't just an update for a single tech portfolio; it serves as a massive, defining diagnostic test on the true state of global artificial intelligence hardware expansion.
We are stepping directly into the ultimate technology toll booth. Because ASML owns a complete, ironclad monopoly over the machines required to manufacture next-generation computing hardware, their financial data tells us exactly what the future looks like before it happens. Let's break down this monopolistic powerhouse section by section, utilizing the exact Wall Street consensus targets and the specific operational metrics that will dictate whether the entire semiconductor sector rallies or experiences an abrupt reality check tomorrow morning.
The Core Moat — Understanding Lithography Dominance
To accurately break down tomorrow's print, you have to look past the stock ticker and explain exactly what this company builds. Silicon Valley loves to talk about advanced AI chips, but there is a massive physical reality that the general public completely glosses over: foundry giants like TSMC, Samsung, and Intel cannot physically print a single advanced AI chip without ASML. ASML designs and manufactures multi-million-dollar Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems. These are essentially massive, hyper-precise cameras that use specialized light beams to print microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers at an atomic scale.
This technology represents the single deepest physical moat in the history of global industry. It takes decades of advanced physics engineering, specialized global supply chains, and billions in capital to construct a single one of these machines. ASML does not merely hold a high market share; they hold a 100% absolute monopoly over the high-end EUV space. If a tech titan wants to build next-generation data centers to run advanced AI models, they are structurally forced to wait in line for an ASML machine. They are the absolute infrastructure gatekeeper of the digital age.
Financial Expectations — Quadrupling Capacity ?
The financial numbers ASML is expected to print tomorrow morning show a technology machine that is completely breaking out of its historical baseline. Institutional desks enter the venue with exceptionally high expectations, looking for an adjusted consensus EPS of $12.13 per share. This represents an explosive ~89% surge year-over-year compared to the $5.49 basic EPS printed in the same quarter last year. On the top line, Wall Street is modeling a consensus revenue target of $13.16 Billion, marking an incredible 51% explosion year-over-year.
When the data flashes across the terminals tomorrow morning, big money will immediately look past the headline numbers to verify whether high-margin EUV machine shipments are successfully defending corporate profit margins against rising input costs. The entire trading reaction will hinge on two primary operational metrics:
– Gross Margin Targets: Management previously guided for a Q3 gross margin ceiling between 55% and 57%. Hitting the upper bound of this target will prove that their extreme monopoly pricing power remains fully intact.
– The Net Bookings Tracker: While reported revenues show past machine deliveries, the absolute true heartbeat of tomorrow's report lies within management's forward-looking order commentary. Analysts are hyper-focused on net bookings for next-generation EUV systems, which serve as the definitive spending blueprint for global foundries entering the 2027 and 2028 manufacturing cycles.
So What About the Future of ASML? — The 2027 Backlog Runway
When you connect the dots across all of their live order books, ASML’s forward-looking fundamental trajectory looks incredibly de-risked. The structural demand for their lithography platforms is tightly insulated because AI model complexity is growing significantly faster than traditional hardware scaling. Every time cloud giants build a larger data center cluster, global foundries are forced to buy more high-NA EUV tools to print smaller, more power-efficient silicon architectures.
This ongoing capacity crunch means ASML is no longer exposed to typical short-term electronic consumer cycles. Their order backlog is heavily filled out through calendar years 2027 and 2028, with major semiconductor manufacturers paying massive upfront deposits just to lock in their factory slots. Management has guided for next-quarter revenue expectations to step up aggressively toward $15.85 Billion, proving that their multi-year growth runway is structurally protected as global tech infrastructure gets completely rebuilt.
The Reality Check — Acknowledging the Operational Risks
Even though the financials and monopolies look extraordinary, the stock market is a two-way street. In this game, you can never guarantee permanent gains, and you must always look closely at the potential risks before entering any financial position. Or, in plain words: enter entirely at your own risk.
The primary risk staring us in the face tomorrow morning centers on strict international export controls and velocity risk. Because ASML's advanced machinery sits at the center of national security infrastructure, tightening global trade restrictions can artificially cap their sales volume into major regional manufacturing hubs. Additionally, while AI chip demand is skyrocketing, legacy consumer chip markets for standard smartphones and PCs are recovering at a much slower pace. Because the stock trades at a premium valuation multiple, any near-term hesitation in their non-AI net bookings will cause short-term momentum funds to aggressively dump shares, leading to sudden, violent technical pullbacks on the chart.
The Bottom Line : Overall Verdict
At the end of the day, tomorrow morning's technology preview is exactly where speculative hype stops and raw operational efficiency takes over. My strategy for this sector is to ignore short-term algorithmic price swings and focus entirely on their underlying net bookings and gross margin discipline. When a company owns a 100% absolute monopoly over the physical plumbing of global computing, an intimidating valuation is simply a reflection of an unbreakable market moat.
I am holding my position with total conviction, tracking the individual machine delivery targets, and letting the core mathematics of the global semiconductor cycle compound my capital over the long horizon.

articles.summary: Samsung Electronics spreads semiconductor bases to prepare for order battles after supply crunch  디지털투데이
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics is spreading its semiconductor research, testing and production bases across Japan, Vietnam and the United States. As AI chip demand prolongs a memory supply crunch and even companies that used to buy chips move into in-house production, the strategy is to build alternative supply sources so customers can receive volumes without disruption. It is also seen as a move to redesign its regional research, testing and production system in preparation for a fight to secure customers after shortages ease, at a time when profits are rising on a memory boom.
Samsung Electronics on Oct. 8 announced preliminary results showing third-quarter operating profit of 10.74 trillion won, up 780 percent from a year earlier. Most of the profit came from memory. Hana Securities analysed that memory operating profit exceeded total profit for the semiconductor division as the display, mobile and home appliance businesses posted small profits or losses and System LSI and foundry operations posted losses. Samsung Electronics is set to release final results including performance by division.
Samsung Electronics' earnings are currently being lifted by higher memory prices, and what is pushing prices up is a supply shortage. According to Hana Securities, third-quarter DRAM prices rose 20 percent from the previous quarter, and customers without long-term supply contracts are paying higher prices. The shortage is likely to continue through 2028 even after accounting for the expansion schedules of the three major DRAM makers.
Companies that used to buy semiconductors are moving into direct production. Hanwha Investment & Securities said Tesla and SpaceX are pursuing an in-house semiconductor fab called TerraFab, judging it difficult to secure stable volumes with capacity expansions by existing foundry and memory makers alone. For customers, whether they can receive volumes on time has become the criterion for choosing a supplier.
Samsung Electronics is responding by placing research, testing and production in different countries. All three are outside South Korea. In Yokohama, Japan, it is building an advanced packaging research base (APL) at a cost of 35 billion yen. It will conduct next-generation chip research, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and 2.5D and 3D packaging, with Japanese materials, components and equipment companies. In Thai Nguyen, Vietnam, it is pursuing a $1.5 billion back-end processing base that will handle pre-shipment inspection and packaging. In Taylor, Texas, it is building an advanced foundry production line linked to subsidies under the U.S. CHIPS Act. It is a base for producing chips directly in the United States, where big tech customers are concentrated.
After memory supply shortages ease, Tesla and SpaceX move into direct chip production.
The three bases target customers that avoid suppliers with production concentrated in one region. TSMC keeps most of its leading-edge process production in Taiwan. It is increasing overseas fabs in the United States and elsewhere, but the centre of advanced chip production remains Taiwan. If variables such as cross-strait tensions or earthquakes arise, customers' chip supply can be shaken together.
Big tech companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft and Meta are therefore looking for suppliers beyond TSMC. With AI chip orders concentrated at one company, they are concerned about rising unit prices and supply delays. Samsung Electronics is seen as seeking to present a system that divides research, testing and production across multiple regions as a condition for an alternative supplier that these customers want.
Beyond memory demand conditions, another reason Samsung Electronics is accelerating is changes in the semiconductor competitive market. While it prepares for supplier competition, new chip makers are also emerging one after another.
According to Hanwha Investment & Securities, Tesla broke ground in April on a $3 billion research fab in Giga Texas, and SpaceX in August confirmed Grimes County, Texas, as the site for a large-scale TerraFab. The first-phase investment alone is more than $16.8 billion. TerraFab combines logic and memory wafer manufacturing, advanced packaging and testing in one base. Unlike traditional contract manufacturing, it allows repeated development from design to testing within a single fab. Initial production will start with Intel's 14A process, and Intel has also made its participation in the project official. That means a chip demand customer is building its own production base in Texas, where Samsung Electronics is building the Taylor fab.
The timing for TerraFab's large-scale mass production has not yet been officially confirmed, but the industry expects full-scale production to begin after 2 to 3 years. Hanwha Investment & Securities forecast that equipment and processes for the mass-production fab will be decided in the meantime. Coincidentally, that timing overlaps with 2028, the peak of the supply shortage. If memory production plans become concrete, the benefits could also spread to South Korean memory supply chains, including Samsung Electronics.
Samsung Electronics' strategy of dispersing bases can also be seen as preparation for which supplier customers will choose after shortages ease. The remaining variable is whether TerraFab will add a new producer to that set of choices. An industry official said the most important factor for big tech companies when selecting a semiconductor foundry is supply chain disruption. "In the past, unit prices and process technology capabilities were important, but now stable operating capacity to receive 100 percent of chips at the desired time is the top priority," the official said.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11162-7Artificial intelligence-enabled quantification and analyses of brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity uncover links between BAT and a healthier metabolic profile along with lower rates of psychiatric disease, and can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate this tissue in humans.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae1,2.
In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat3.
Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases4.
However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking5,6.
Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre.
Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT.
Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution.
People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices.
Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence.
As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure.
Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

Main
Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension and cardiovascular disease2,7. Adipose tissue dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity and contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiometabolic diseases1. White adipose tissue (WAT) stores energy as triglyceride1 in subcutaneous and visceral depots, and visceral adiposity is a key feature of metabolically unhealthy obesity8. By contrast, brown adipose tissue (BAT) dissipates energy as heat (thermogenesis) and its activation in animal models protects against obesity and metabolic diseases3. However, the relevance of BAT to adult human physiology and whether it can be targeted therapeutically remain unclear5,6.
Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT9,10,11,12, several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists13,14,15,16,17. Although these interventions activate BAT and improve glucose homeostasis, their side effects and the small number of participants studied have limited their clinical impact5. More recently, our group described the largest reported cohort of people with BAT and demonstrated that the presence of BAT in 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)–computed tomography (CT) (18F-FDG-PET–CT) scans obtained for clinical purposes and without previous stimulation was associated with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease4. A caveat from this work is that patients were characterized based on BAT presence or absence, rather than by quantitative BAT metabolic activity. Like WAT, human BAT is localized in distinct anatomic depots18, but whether these depots uniquely affect health remains unknown. Moreover, most human BAT studies have focused on cardiometabolic outcomes, but how this tissue influences other organ systems and disease types remains largely unexplored. These limitations have hindered the identification of pharmacologic agents that promote BAT activity, and there are no approved, widely used medications to leverage the cardiometabolic benefits linked to this tissue.
In this study we expanded our cohort to more than 100,000 patients and performed an unbiased, comprehensive analysis across all diagnostic codes to identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT presence. Furthermore, we harnessed artificial intelligence (AI) to semi-automatically quantify total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity from 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans. This allowed us to investigate associations between specific BAT depots, WAT distribution and cardiometabolic outcomes. Finally, we combined these approaches with medication use analyses to identify pharmacologic regulators of BAT and performed proof-of-concept experiments to validate losartan as an activator of brown adipocytes through a unique, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ)-dependent mechanism.
Associations of BAT with all diagnoses
To discover associations between BAT and diseases beyond the cardiometabolic system, we expanded our previously described cohort (Established BAT Cohort)4 by reviewing additional FDG-PET–CT scans taken from 2018 to 2024 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Of these, 4.4% reported BAT presence and 4,778 patients (7.9%) had at least one scan positive for BAT (hereafter termed BAT positive (BAT+); Extended Data Fig. 1a). The remaining patients were designated BAT negative (BAT−). These newly identified participants were grouped in an Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a) that validated findings from our Established BAT Cohort4 demonstrating lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases in people who are BAT+ (Extended Data Fig. 1b). To increase statistical power, we merged the Established and Extension BAT Cohorts to create an Expanded BAT Cohort, consisting of 101,243 patients, of whom 8,897 were BAT+ and 92,346 were BAT−. Each patient was assigned an index scan as a reference point for clinical data collection (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Similar to previous findings4, BAT was more prevalent in women in the Expanded BAT Cohort, and its prevalence decreased with age, higher ambient temperature at the time of the scan and increasing body mass index (BMI) (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f).
Given the influence of these variables on BAT prevalence, we used propensity score matching (PSM) to create a cohort of patients in the BAT+ (n = 8,897) and BAT− (n = 17,405) groups balanced across age, sex, BMI and ambient temperature (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). As patients in our cohort come from a cancer centre, we extracted extensive cancer-associated data (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2) for each patient in our PSM cohort, including site, stage and treatment. We confirmed that certain cancer sites were more frequent (for example, breast and oral cavity), less frequent (for example, digestive) or had no association (for example, skin, urinary) with BAT presence (Table 1). As in our previous report, some cancer treatments were used more frequently in the BAT+ group4 (Table 1). Consequently, all cancer-associated variables were controlled for unless otherwise stated for the remainder of this study. We then performed multi-variable logistic regression in this new, expanded PSM cohort and confirmed the association between BAT presence and decreased prevalence of select cardiometabolic diseases4 (Extended Data Fig. 1i). Given the sexual dimorphism in BAT presence and cardiometabolic traits, we performed separate analyses in women and men and found that BAT was associated with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases in both sexes in our PSM and Extension BAT Cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b).
Next, we used an unbiased approach to establish associations between BAT and diseases across all organ systems in our PSM cohort (Fig. 1a). After extraction of International Classification of Diseases (ICD) code data and initial screening analysis (Fig. 1a), 104 of 511 codes exhibited significant, non-adjusted associations with BAT (Supplementary Table 3). Over-representation analysis revealed that cardiovascular and psychiatric diagnoses were enriched significantly in their association with BAT (Fig. 1b). We then ran a multi-variable logistic regression for each of the 104 codes to establish associations with BAT, adjusting for multiple co-variates. This resulted in 98 codes that were significant after adjustment, with 92 showing lower incidence in patients in the BAT+ group (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4).
Among the top 20 codes with lower prevalence in the BAT+ group, the two most significant were T2D (odds ratio (OR) 0.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.35–0.50; P < 0.001) and chronic ischaemic heart disease (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.44–0.62; P < 0.001); other cardiometabolic codes such as disorders of lipoprotein metabolism (OR 0.76; 95% CI 0.70–0.83; P < 0.001) and primary hypertension (OR 0.79; 95% CI 0.73–0.85; P < 0.001) were also present. We also identified associations with other disease systems, including decreased odds of respiratory failure (OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.37–0.57; P < 0.001), ascites (OR 0.51; 95% CI 0.43–0.62; P < 0.001), anxiety disorders (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.73–0.84; P < 0.001), depressive episode (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.61–0.76; P < 0.001) and sleep disorders (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.71–0.85; P < 0.001) in patients who were BAT+ (Fig. 1c). Among codes with higher prevalence in the BAT+ group, five of six were skin diagnoses (Extended Data Fig. 2c). BAT+ status also trended toward being associated with a higher prevalence of osteoporosis, although this did not reach statistical significance in the adjusted analysis (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Global Adoption of AI
The latest AI stats on organizational adoption tell a clear story: AI is no longer the technology that businesses are experimenting with. It is ingrained in the way organizations are run, the way individuals work, and to an increasing degree, the way people live. The artificial intelligence stats make this shift hard to ignore.
Organizations (%) Using AI
- The 2025 AI Index Report by Stanford HAI indicates that 78% of organizations worldwide used AI in 2024, a steep increase from 55% the previous year
- This is supported by Explodingtopics data, which indicates an identical 78% in 2025 and 90% of companies actively using or exploring it
It is not an upward slope; that is a leap, indicative of the pace at which AI is shifting from pilot projects to infrastructure. The enterprise tier also looks promising.
- More than 42% of businesses with over 1,000 employees have implemented AI [Source: IBM Newsroom]
- At the highest level, 99% of the Fortune 500 companies already apply AI in some way, the most apparent being the hiring and HR procedures [Source: Qualtrics]
- Generative AI has also passed a material milestone: 71% of businesses are now utilizing it in at least one business operation [Source: Stanford]
Population (%) Using Generative AI Tools
Consumer-level adoption is growing fast, but it's still early days globally.
- In their H2 2025 AI Economy report, Microsoft reported that global adoption of generative AI is 16.3% of the working-age population, up from 15.1% in the first half of the year
- In the U.S., the St. Louis Fed found that generative AI use for work-related tasks was 37.4% and for non-work applications was 48.7% as of 2025, both higher than PC adoption was at the same stage post-launch
Trends by Region and Industry

- The UAE (64%) and Singapore (60.9%) are the first and second most prevalent in the use of generative AI (diffusion) among their working-age populations [Source: Microsoft]
- The global North is at 24.7% adoption, about two times marginally higher than the global South at 14.1%, reflecting a growing gap in AI access that mirrors existing infrastructural gaps [Source: Microsoft]
Across industries,
- The technology sector predictably leads with 78% overall AI tool usage
- Financial services at 71%
- Healthcare at 64%
- Manufacturing at 59%
- Retail at 56%
- And education at 52%
Government adoption (48%) tends to lag due to regulatory and procurement complexity. India holds the distinction of having the highest AI adoption among individual countries, with about 59% of companies, which is higher than in most Western economies. [Source: Worklytics]

articles.full_text:
CATL remains the world’s largest electric vehicle battery supplier in 2026, ahead of BYD and LG Energy Solution. However, the competition extends beyond market share: battery prices, manufacturing efficiency, customer diversification and regional demand are determining which suppliers can grow profitably.
Global battery installations reached 844.2 gigawatt-hours from January through August 2026, increasing 19.7 percent year on year. The figures cover batteries installed in registered battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hybrid electric vehicles, rather than total battery production.
For automakers, supplier selection connects vehicle affordability with dependable delivery, charging performance and long-term warranty support.
CATL and BYD together supplied approximately 460.9 GWh, accounting for roughly 54.6 percent of installations. Seven Chinese suppliers held a combined 73.3 percent share.
Growth varied sharply: CATL increased installations 25.2 percent, Gotion 47.1 percent, EVE 53.9 percent and REPT 126.3 percent. BYD grew 6.2 percent, while SK On declined 14.5 percent. These are eight-month results, not full-year rankings from Insight -SNE Research.
CATL Combines Market Leadership With Financial Strength
CATL’s 2025 annual results, released in March 2026, reported revenue of RMB 423.7 billion, up 17 percent, and net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 72.2 billion, up 42 percent.
Lithium-ion battery sales reached 661 GWh, increasing 39 percent. These sales include applications beyond electric vehicles and therefore differ from SNE’s automotive installation figures.
CATL reported 772 GWh of production capacity, with another 321 GWh under construction at year-end. Research and development spending reached RMB 22.1 billion, approximately 5.2 percent of revenue.
The company also processed 210,000 tonnes of spent batteries and regenerated 24,000 tonnes of lithium salts.
The combination of earnings, research spending and manufacturing scale gives CATL resources to develop products and expand internationally. Its challenge is to bring additional capacity online at a pace that matches commercially viable demand.
BYD’s Integrated Model Creates a Different Advantage
BYD combines battery manufacturing with vehicle production, allowing battery design and vehicle engineering to develop within the same group.
Its Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. LFP avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode and is widely used where cost, durability and thermal stability are priorities.
BYD’s structure can simplify coordination between vehicle platforms and battery supply. However, it also means battery deployment is closely linked to the performance of its own automotive business.
For buyers comparing BYD with independent suppliers, the relevant questions extend beyond installation volumes. External supply availability, platform compatibility, commercial terms and production location determine whether a battery offering fits an automaker’s requirements.
LG Energy Solution, Panasonic and SK On Face Different Demand Exposure
LG Energy Solution and Panasonic recorded installation growth below the overall market, while SK On’s volumes contracted.
These suppliers remain important because of their established vehicle programmes and manufacturing relationships. Their results illustrate how customer concentration and regional exposure can influence performance even when worldwide battery demand rises.
The International Energy Agency notes that Tesla continues sourcing most of its EV batteries from established suppliers including Panasonic, LG Energy Solution and CATL, despite developing its own manufacturing capabilities.
For suppliers, winning a vehicle programme creates an opportunity rather than a guaranteed production volume. Actual demand depends on vehicle sales, launch schedules and the customer’s decisions about battery sourcing.
Battery Prices Show Why Chemistry Matters
BloombergNEF’s 2025 battery price survey provides a cost benchmark for evaluating the market in 2026.
Average lithium-ion pack prices fell 8 percent to $108 per kilowatt-hour. Battery-electric vehicle packs averaged $99/kWh, while chemistry averages across applications were $81/kWh for LFP and $128/kWh for nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries.
Using those chemistry averages, an illustrative 60 kWh pack would cost approximately $4,860 with LFP or $7,680 with NMC—a difference of $2,820. This calculation is not a supplier quotation or a comparison of otherwise identical packs.
China’s regional average was $84/kWh. North American and European prices were 44 percent and 56 percent higher, respectively, implying approximately $121/kWh and $131/kWh.
Stationary-storage packs averaged $70/kWh, down 45 percent, demonstrating why automotive and storage battery prices should be compared separately.
Lower Battery Costs Do Not Automatically Mean Cheaper Cars
Battery purchasing costs influence vehicle economics, but retail prices also reflect manufacturing, electronics, distribution, taxes and financing.
For an illustrative 75 kWh vehicle, a $10/kWh reduction in pack cost represents $750 in potential manufacturing savings. An automaker could use that saving to lower prices, improve margins or fund additional features.
Likewise, a lower-priced chemistry is not automatically the best choice for every model. Energy density, pack size, charging behaviour and vehicle weight affect the final design.
Suppliers that offer several suitable products can address more vehicle categories, while automakers must evaluate the complete battery system rather than the cell price alone.
Manufacturing Capacity Exceeds 4 TWh
The IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 battery analysis reports that global lithium-ion nameplate manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 terawatt-hours at the end of 2025, up approximately 30 percent.
China accounted for more than 80 percent of capacity, while the European Union and United States each represented approximately 6–7 percent.
The IEA projects EV battery deployment approaching 3 TWh in 2030 under both its Current Policies and Stated Policies scenarios, compared with approximately 1.2 TWh in 2025.
Capacity and demand figures cover different scopes, so their ratio should not be treated as an industry utilization rate. Moreover, a completed factory must qualify products, improve yields and secure orders before it can deliver dependable commercial output.
What Will Determine Future Battery Supplier Leadership?
CATL leads on automotive installations, while BYD benefits from its integrated vehicle-and-battery model. Chinese challengers are expanding rapidly, and established Korean and Japanese suppliers remain central to many international vehicle programmes.
Future leadership will depend on profitable production, reliable quality and diversified customers. Recycling, regional manufacturing and new chemistries can strengthen competitiveness, but each requires commercially workable processes.
For automakers, the strongest supplier relationship combines competitive lifetime costs with consistent delivery, suitable performance and credible warranty support. Installation rankings show current scale; sustained returns and dependable execution will determine which battery manufacturers retain their advantage.
SHAFANA FAZAL

articles.title: Satellite Network A 'Geopolitical Control Tool': Think Tank Seeks Starlink Curbs - Deccan Chronicle

articles.full_text:
The report calls for India to retain control over domestic data flows, network access and emergency shutdowns, while accelerating development of an indigenous satellite constellation.
Starlink, owned by the world's richest man Elon Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install. It has been trying to enter India since 2021 and secured key licences in June 2025 and authorisation from space regulator IN-SAPCe the following month. It, however, hasn't been able to launch services pending final security clearances and spectrum allocation.
Outstanding issues include security clearances, foreign-investment approval and the framework for allocating spectrum. Officials are also examining whether inter-satellite links could allow Indian traffic to bypass domestic gateways.
Frustrated at the delay, Musk last week alleged that "oligarchs" were blocking Starlink's entry into India - an allegation the Ministry of Communications rejected as baseless.
The ministry said three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
Kutniti points to SpaceX's contracts with the US defence and intelligence establishments as evidence that satellite communications have strategic as well as commercial applications. It cites a USD 70 million Pentagon task order for Starshield services and a reported classified contract with the National Reconnaissance Office to develop a network of reconnaissance satellites.
The report argues that the combination of satellite infrastructure, ground gateways and foreign legal jurisdiction creates potential vulnerabilities for countries dependent on the service. It raises concerns about whether Indian communications could be exposed to foreign intelligence collection and whether New Delhi would have sufficient control over network operations during a security crisis.
The report cites Ukraine's experience as an example of how dependence on privately operated satellite communications can affect military operations.
Starlink became a critical communications service following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, supporting civilian connectivity and military communications. But disputes over the geographical availability and military use of the network also highlighted the influence an operator can exercise over access.
In March 2025, Musk wrote: "My Starlink system is the backbone of the Ukrainian army. Their entire front line would collapse if I turned it off."
The report also points to regulatory disputes in Brazil, South Africa, Namibia and Taiwan. In Brazil, Starlink initially resisted an order to block access to the social-media platform X before complying after its accounts were frozen.
The report recommends that any foreign low-Earth-orbit operator be required to route all Indian traffic through gateways in India, with no bypass via inter-satellite links. They should also register terminals and let India hold its own auditable on/off capability.
Lawful interception and data localisation under Indian law alone, shielded from the US CLOUD Act and FISA Section 702, should be a precondition, it said, adding operators must be contractually barred from withdrawing service unilaterally during a declared emergency, with penalties held in escrow.
The report cites Taiwan as a precedent for requiring foreign satellite operators to meet domestic ownership and security conditions. It says Taiwan's July 2026 legislative changes allow case-by-case exemptions from foreign-ownership limits, subject to national-security considerations and conditions including domestic infrastructure.
Kutniti argues that India, with its large telecommunications market and established space programme, has substantial bargaining power.
Kutniti warns that a dominant global satellite operator could weaken investment in India's private space sector by competing across satellite communications, Earth observation and launch services.
The report argues that if investors favour an established international provider with a large constellation and frequent launch capability, Indian start-ups could struggle to secure funding for their own satellites and services. Reduced demand for domestic payloads could then weaken the broader ecosystem, including launch vehicles and related manufacturing.
The foundation says roughly USD 1 billion has already been invested in India's emerging space industry across start-ups, public-sector entities and large companies. It urges the government to build an indigenous mega-constellation before 2029, arguing that domestic infrastructure would support national security, technological independence and export opportunities.
The report also warns that satellite-to-mobile, or direct-to-cell, services could intensify competition for Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel and state-run BSNL as satellite networks expand beyond traditional broadband.

Why in News?
A public dispute over Starlink’s proposed entry into India’s satellite internet market has raised concerns regarding market competition, regulatory approvals, national security and consumer affordability, highlighting the challenges surrounding the expansion of satellite-based internet services in India.
What are the Key Facts About Starlink?
- About Starlink: Starlink is a satellite-based broadband internet service developed by SpaceX. It uses a constellation of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites to provide high-speed, low-latency internet connectivity, particularly in remote and underserved regions.
- Satellite Constellation: Starlink operates the world's largest commercial satellite constellation, with approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit as of October 2026, primarily operating at altitudes of around 550 km, compared to 35,786 km for geostationary satellites.
- Advanced Technology: Starlink satellites use optical inter-satellite links (space lasers), phased-array antennas and argon-powered ion thrusters to enable high-speed data transmission, satellite-to-satellite communication and orbital manoeuvring.
- Low-Latency Connectivity: Starlink offers latency of around 25 milliseconds under favourable conditions, compared with approximately 600 milliseconds or more for traditional geostationary satellite internet, supporting video calls, online gaming and streaming.
- SpaceX Integration: SpaceX manufactures and operates Starlink satellites and uses its Falcon 9 launch vehicles to regularly deploy and upgrade the constellation, supporting continuous network expansion.
- Strategic and Humanitarian Applications: Starlink provides connectivity in remote areas, disaster-affected regions and conflict zones where terrestrial communication networks are unavailable, damaged or disrupted.
- Military Applications: SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a separate military-focused satellite communications programme for US government and national security applications.
What is the Status of Starlink’s Licence in India?
- GMPCS Licence: Starlink received a Unified Licence with Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) authorisation from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) in June 2025, permitting satellite communication services subject to regulatory conditions.
- IN-SPACe Authorisation: In July 2025, Starlink also received authorisation from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) for its satellite constellation.
- Pending Clearances: Despite these approvals, Starlink has not commenced commercial services in India, as final security clearances, spectrum assignment and other regulatory requirements remain pending.
- Commercial Partnerships: In March 2025, SpaceX signed separate agreements with Jio Platforms and Bharti Airtel to explore distributing Starlink services in India, subject to the necessary regulatory approvals.
- Current Status: Starlink holds key telecommunications and space-sector authorisations but cannot launch commercial satellite internet services in India until the remaining security and spectrum-related requirements are fulfilled.
How Does Satellite Internet Work?
- About: Satellite internet is a communication technology that uses orbiting satellites to provide broadband connectivity, particularly in remote, sparsely populated and disaster-prone regions where terrestrial networks are economically unviable or unavailable.
- Working Mechanism: Satellite internet operates through two main segments: 
  - Space Segment: Consists of satellites equipped with communication payloads that receive, process or relay data signals between Earth-based terminals and ground stations.
  - Ground Segment: Comprises user terminals (antennas and modems) and ground stations that communicate with satellites and connect users to the internet backbone.
- Orbital Deployment: Communication satellites are deployed in three main orbital regions: 
  - Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO): Located approximately 35,786 km above the equator, GEO satellites remain stationary relative to Earth and provide extensive coverage, but their high latency limits performance in time-sensitive applications. Example: Inmarsat Global Xpress (GX).
  - Medium Earth Orbit (MEO): Located between approximately 2,000 km and 35,786 km, MEO satellites offer lower latency than GEO satellites but require constellations for wider coverage. Example: O3b constellation.
  - Low Earth Orbit (LEO): Located below 2,000 km, LEO satellites provide low-latency connectivity but have smaller individual coverage areas, requiring large constellations for continuous coverage. Example: Starlink.
- Mega-Constellation Technology: Advanced LEO constellations use onboard signal processing, phased-array antennas and optical inter-satellite links (space lasers) to enable direct satellite-to-satellite communication, efficient data routing and seamless connectivity as satellites move across the sky.
- Applications: Satellite internet supports connectivity in remote regions, disaster management, telemedicine, precision agriculture, maritime and aviation communications, military operations and emergency response.
- Challenges: Despite its advantages, satellite internet faces challenges such as high equipment and subscription costs, orbital congestion, space debris, cybersecurity risks and national security concerns associated with its dual-use civilian and military applications.
Frequently Asked Questions(FAQs)
1. What is Starlink?
Starlink is a satellite-based broadband internet service developed by SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk. It uses a constellation of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites to provide high-speed, low-latency internet connectivity, particularly in remote and underserved regions. 
2. Why is Starlink in the news in India?
Starlink has attracted attention following a public dispute between Elon Musk and Mukesh Ambani over competition and regulatory barriers in India's satellite internet market, raising concerns about market access, national security and consumer affordability. 
3. Has Starlink received permission to operate in India?
Starlink has received GMPCS authorisation from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and authorisation from IN-SPACe. However, commercial services have not commenced because additional security requirements and spectrum assignment remain pending. 
4. What is GMPCS authorisation?
Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) authorisation permits operators to provide satellite-based communication services in India, subject to prescribed licensing, security and regulatory conditions. 
5. What is the role of IN-SPACe in satellite internet services?
The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) is responsible for authorising and facilitating non-government space activities, including the operation of satellite constellations serving India.

The impact of Starlink and Starshield on Ukraine's digital sovereignty
Technological innovation or geopolitical risk? The duality of Starlink and Starshield
Starlink vs. Starshield: The digital battle for control of communications
The debate surrounding satellite-based communications, particularly between Starlink and Starshield, has gained urgency in recent years against the backdrop of the Ukraine conflict. These two systems, which emerged from the SpaceX ecosystem, are not only at the center of technological debates but have also become central components of geopolitical strategies. Starlink, as a commercial platform, offers a wide range of internet services for households and businesses, while Starshield focuses on state security and defense needs. These differences between the two systems are not merely technical but also concern issues of control, accountability, and the geopolitical implications arising from their use. Ukraine serves as a prime example in this context: it demonstrates how digital infrastructure is not neutral in war but rather serves as a tool for power, security, and strategic decision-making. This analysis examines how Starlink and Starshield influence the digital sovereignty of modern states, the challenges arising from their use, and the lessons Europe can learn from these developments.
Starlink, Starshield and the price of dependence
Whoever controls the data stream controls more than just the network in a worst-case scenario
The controversy surrounding restrictions on satellite-based communication in Ukraine demonstrates that digital infrastructure in warfare is neither neutral nor purely technical. It is simultaneously a means of production, a security guarantee, a political lever, and an integral part of military operations. At the heart of this debate are two names that are frequently conflated: Starlink and Starshield. Both originate from the SpaceX ecosystem, utilize related technologies, and leverage the advantages of large satellite arrays in low Earth orbit. However, economically, institutionally, and strategically, they are not the same.
Starlink is essentially a commercial communications platform. The system sells internet access to private households, businesses, mobility providers, and public institutions. Starshield, on the other hand, targets government security, defense, and intelligence clients. This not only shifts the user base but also changes the requirements for encryption, control, licensing, operational profiles, contract design, and political accountability. Starlink primarily follows the logic of a scalable platform business, while Starshield more closely aligns with the logic of government-funded security infrastructure.
The crucial question, therefore, is not simply which system is technically more powerful. More important is who decides on access rights, geographical permissions, speed limits, prioritization, and permissible applications. It is precisely at this point that private property rights, government procurement contracts, military chains of command, and foreign policy interests collide. Ukraine is not merely an isolated case. It is the most visible example of a fundamental problem facing modern states: Critical capabilities are increasingly being provided via privately developed and operated digital platforms, even though their failures can have immediate consequences for national security, the economy, and human lives.
A technological family tree with two business logics
Starlink and Starshield are based on a shared industrial foundation. SpaceX develops satellites, manufactures them in large quantities, organizes launches, operates ground infrastructure, and manages the network. This vertical integration is a significant competitive advantage. A company that largely controls launch vehicles, satellites, terminals, software, and network operations in-house can scale up capacity more quickly and implement technical changes faster than providers that rely on external partners at every stage.
Starlink leverages this foundation for a global broadband offering. Thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit form a distributed network through which user terminals send and receive data. The comparatively short distance to Earth reduces signal propagation time compared to traditional geostationary satellites. This enables applications that require not only high bandwidth but also short response times. These include video conferencing, cloud access, real-time communication, mobile connections, and certain control and sensor services.
Starshield adopts key elements of this modular system but is designed for government missions. These include secure communications, Earth observation, and the hosting of specialized payloads on satellite platforms. The difference, therefore, lies not simply in a different tariff or a more robustly designed terminal. Starshield can incorporate custom satellites, additional cryptographic methods, classified payloads, specialized ground architectures, and government-defined operating procedures. It is more accurate to speak of a family of government solutions than of a single, universally identical military network.
The often-used shorthand that Starshield is simply the military version of Starlink is therefore catchy but incomplete. It underestimates the range of possible contract and system configurations. In one case, a state might procure secure communication services on a related network architecture. In another, purpose-built satellites and sensors might be part of a state-controlled system. Technical origin, legal ownership, operational control, and political decision-making power must be considered separately.
Starlink as a scalable platform business
Economically, Starlink relies on high initial investments and sharply declining average costs as utilization increases. Satellite development, production, rocket launches, ground stations, frequency rights, software, and network monitoring require billions of dollars. However, once the infrastructure is in place, every additional paying connection can contribute to covering these fixed costs. This is similar to platform and telecommunications models, but with one key difference: satellites have a limited lifespan and must be replaced regularly. The network is therefore not a one-time investment, but rather an industrial fleet that requires continuous renewal.
The civilian mass market is central to this calculation. Millions of connections spread the costs across a broad customer base. At the same time, Starlink taps into higher-priced segments such as aviation, shipping, enterprise, government, and mobile services. This mix improves revenue quality. Households provide volume, while institutional and mobile customers can pay higher prices for prioritization, coverage, service guarantees, or specialized hardware.
Furthermore, there is an internal economies of scale between space travel and communications. SpaceX can launch its own satellites with its own rockets. A high launch frequency reduces the cost per mission through experience, reuse, and better utilization. Starlink, in turn, creates a continuous demand for launches. This stabilizes the utilization of the rocket infrastructure, while cheaper launches facilitate network expansion. This feedback loop is difficult to replicate and explains a significant part of the advantage over traditional satellite operators.
The business model remains capital-intensive and risky. A growing fleet necessitates replacement investments, monitoring costs, and regulatory burdens. In affluent regions, Starlink competes with fiber optics, cable, and high-performance mobile networks. In poorer or sparsely populated markets, demand is high, but purchasing power is often limited. Economic success therefore depends on acquiring enough high-paying customers in underserved areas and securing high-margin institutional applications.
Starshield as a state-funded security economy
Starshield operates on a different revenue and risk structure. Government customers don't simply buy bandwidth. They pay for availability, security of classified information, mission-specific customization, controlled supply chains, specialized encryption, and integration with military or intelligence systems. Therefore, value stems less from maximum user numbers than from strategic importance and demanding requirements.
In this market, contracts are often longer-term, more complex, and politically sensitive. Development risks can be partially mitigated by government payments. At the same time, documentation requirements, safety regulations, export controls, and dependencies on budgetary decisions are increasing. A supplier can generate high revenues with relatively few clients but faces a significant concentration risk. If a major government client changes priorities, cuts programs, or tightens usage rules, this has a direct impact on the business.
From a government perspective, Starshield is attractive because it allows the use of existing industrial economies of scale. Instead of developing each satellite platform from scratch, proven components, mass production, and frequent launches can be used. This shortens development times and can reduce the cost per unit. Furthermore, a large number of smaller satellites increases resilience to the failure of individual units. In security economics, this shifts the model from a few extremely expensive large satellites to distributed constellations with faster renewal.
This efficiency, however, comes at an institutional price. The more government agencies depend on the production capacity, launch infrastructure, and software of a single company, the greater its structural bargaining power becomes. articles.title: GlobalFoundries to Operate Two New Semiconductor Fabs in New York Under $21B U.S.-Japan Deal - Construction Review

GlobalFoundries has been selected to operate two proposed semiconductor fabrication plants in Malta, New York, under a U.S.-Japan initiative providing up to $21 billion in investment to expand U.S. chip manufacturing capacity.
Announced on October 14, 2026, the initiative will see Japan provide the investment capital, while GlobalFoundries supplies the technology and operational expertise. The first fab is expected to receive approximately $10 billion, with construction expected to begin later in 2026 and operations targeted for 2029. A second fab would require an additional investment of approximately $10 billion.
The initiative forms part of a broader U.S.-Japan investment agreement under which Japan committed to invest $550 billion in the United States.
GlobalFoundries’ New Semiconductor Fabs in New York
The first facility is expected to add approximately 900,000 300-millimeter wafers of annual manufacturing capacity. If both fabs proceed, their combined capacity could reach 1.8 million wafers annually.
The overall initiative is projected to generate approximately 27,000 construction and semiconductor-industry ecosystem jobs, alongside more than 1,000 high-skilled manufacturing jobs in New York’s Capital Region, according to GlobalFoundries.
According to Reuters, initial customers for the new facilities include Apple and Japan’s Renesas Electronics. General Motors and Cirrus Logic are also part of GlobalFoundries’ wider customer ecosystem, although their existing relationships do not confirm production allocations at the new fabs.
The facilities are expected to be jointly owned by U.S. and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries, which will earn fees for providing technology and manufacturing services. The company has also expressed interest in involving Japanese equipment suppliers such as Tokyo Electron, although specific procurement contracts have not been announced.
Separate $955 Million CHIPS Act Amendment
Alongside the new-fab initiative, the U.S. Department of Commerce amended GlobalFoundries’ existing CHIPS and Science Act award, reallocating up to $955 million in incentives to support $5 billion in investment at its existing facilities in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont.
The amendment does not increase the total federal award. The investment will support silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe) and advanced packaging technologies used in communications infrastructure, data centers and high-performance computing.
This federal agreement is separate from Japan’s funding for the two proposed new fabs.
U.S. Government to Increase Its GlobalFoundries Stake
According to Reuters, GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen said the U.S. government would acquire an additional 4% stake in the company, bringing its total ownership to approximately 7%.
The equity arrangement is separate from the ownership structure of the new facilities. GlobalFoundries remains majority-owned by Mubadala Investment Company, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund.
Advanced Packaging and Related Investments
On October 8, 2026, GlobalFoundries announced a separate multiyear $2 billion agreement with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) to manufacture silicon interposers at its Malta facility for TSMC’s advanced packaging ecosystem. These components connect processors and memory chips within advanced packages used in high-performance computing and AI systems.
GlobalFoundries also announced a $16 billion U.S. investment plan in June 2025 covering its New York and Vermont operations. These investments should not automatically be added to the new initiative’s total because their scopes and funding arrangements differ.
Project factsheet: GlobalFoundries new fabs in New York
- Project: Two proposed semiconductor fabs.
- Location: Malta, Saratoga County, New York.
- Operator: GlobalFoundries.
- Announcement: October 14, 2026.
- Potential investment: Up to $21 billion from the U.S.-Japan initiative.
- First fab: Approximately $10 billion; operations targeted for 2029.
- Second fab: Approximately $10 billion, subject to additional investment.
- Capacity: Approximately 900,000 wafers annually per fab.
- Projected employment: 27,000 construction and ecosystem jobs, plus more than 1,000 high-skilled manufacturing jobs.
- Initial customers: Apple and Renesas Electronics, according to Reuters.
- Separate federal investment: $5 billion at existing facilities, supported by an amendment reallocating up to $955 million in existing CHIPS Act incentives.
- U.S. government ownership: Expected to rise to approximately 7%, according to Reuters.
- Majority owner: Mubadala Investment Company.
The GlobalFoundries expansion complements semiconductor research investments such as Applied Materials’ approximately $5 billion EPIC Center in Silicon Valley, California. Unveiled on October 12, 2026, the 600,000-square-foot research and development facility aims to accelerate the development and commercialization of next-generation chipmaking equipment and processes. While GlobalFoundries’ proposed fabs focus on manufacturing capacity, the EPIC Center focuses on technology development, addressing another part of the semiconductor supply chain as demand for AI chips and advanced computing grows.

President Trump’s agreement with Japan unlocks up to $21 billion investment to expand foundational semiconductor production, support American jobs and strengthen domestic supply chains

Enabled by President Donald J. Trump’s trade and investment agreement with Japan, the initiative will accelerate trusted semiconductor manufacturing in the United States, strengthen critical supply chains and support growing demand across automotive, industrial and connected infrastructure markets.
Japan will provide the investment, while GF will contribute its differentiated technologies, manufacturing expertise and proven operational capabilities as technology provider and operator.
An initial investment of approximately $10 billion will accelerate construction of a new 300mm semiconductor fab, which is expected to come online in 2029. An additional investment of approximately $10 billion would fund a second fab. Together, the two fabs will add significant new U.S. manufacturing capacity and reinforce GF’s ability to support customers worldwide.
“This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the United States and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” said Tim Breen, CEO of GlobalFoundries. “GF was selected because fabs of this scale require more than capital. They require differentiated technology, operational excellence and a proven ability to execute. That combination is what positions GF to make this first-of-its-kind initiative a success.”
The first fab is expected to add approximately 900,000 300mm wafers of annual U.S. manufacturing capacity when fully operational. A second fab would add approximately the same amount. The project is expected to create about 27,000 construction and ecosystem jobs and more than 1,000 high-skilled manufacturing jobs in New York’s Capital Region.

This is a milestone for our employees, our region and the future of advanced manufacturing in New York.”

This new investment will help accelerate the advanced semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem in the United States.”

articles.title: ASML Earnings Beat Forecasts as AI Chip Demand Exceeds Planned Supply Through 2028 - Markets.com
articles.summary: ASML Earnings Beat Forecasts as AI Chip Demand Exceeds Planned Supply Through 2028  Markets.com
articles.full_text:
ASML reported record third-quarter profit and raised its full-year sales outlook as chipmakers accelerated equipment purchases to meet rapidly expanding demand for artificial-intelligence processors.
The Dutch semiconductor-equipment company generated €11.66 billion in revenue and €4.96 billion in net income during the third quarter. Its gross margin climbed to 57.5%, exceeding both company guidance and market expectations.
Basic earnings reached €12.95 per share, compared with €7.59 in the second quarter. Expressed in US dollars, earnings were approximately $14.50 per American depositary receipt, comfortably above the $12.17 Wall Street estimate.
However, ASML’s US-listed shares fell approximately 3.8% to $1,650. Revenue narrowly missed some analyst forecasts, while concerns about high technology valuations and rising interest rates weighed on the broader semiconductor sector.
ASML’s third-quarter revenue increased approximately 55% from €7.52 billion a year earlier and 25% from the second quarter.
Net income more than doubled from roughly €2.13 billion in the third quarter of 2025 and rose 70% sequentially. Gross profit reached €6.7 billion, producing the company’s strongest margin in recent quarters.
| Q3 2026 metric | Reported | Q2 2026 | Market expectation | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Net sales | €11.66 billion | €9.33 billion | Around €11.7 billion | 
| Net income | €4.96 billion | €2.92 billion | Around €4.1 billion | 
| Basic EPS | €12.95 | €7.59 | Around €10.87 | 
| Gross margin | 57.5% | 54.0% | Approximately 56% | 
| Installed Base Management sales | €3.29 billion | €2.76 billion | Below reported result | 
The quarter was not a completely clean beat. Revenue came in slightly below the €11.71 billion to €11.85 billion range reflected in several analyst surveys. The shortfall was small, however, and was offset by much stronger profitability.
Part of the profit increase came from an approximately €500 million revaluation gain related to ASML’s investment in French artificial-intelligence company Mistral AI. Even allowing for that benefit, the underlying result remained strong because gross margin substantially exceeded expectations.
Installed Base Management revenue reached €3.29 billion, almost €400 million above ASML’s guidance.
The business includes maintenance, software, field options and productivity upgrades for lithography equipment already operating in customers’ factories. These services generally produce higher margins than selling newly manufactured systems.
Chipmakers are upgrading existing EUV and deep ultraviolet machines to increase wafer output while they wait for additional systems. That demand helped ASML’s gross margin rise from 54% in the second quarter to 57.5%.
Net system sales totaled approximately €8.4 billion. EUV equipment generated around €4.1 billion, including revenue from one High-NA EUV system, while non-EUV machines contributed approximately €4.3 billion.
ASML recognized sales of 113 new lithography systems, up from 86 in the second quarter, as well as eight used systems.
| Systems sold | Q3 2026 | Q2 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| New lithography systems | 113 | 86 | 
| Used lithography systems | 8 | 5 | 
The higher shipment volume illustrates how quickly ASML is increasing production. The more significant development, however, was management’s warning that its current expansion plans are still insufficient.
ASML said customers continue to raise their short- and medium-term equipment forecasts because they now expect AI infrastructure investment to remain elevated for longer.
Based on those updated forecasts, the company no longer expects its planned production capacity to meet customer demand in either 2027 or 2028.
ASML previously planned to increase production capacity for Low-NA EUV and DUV immersion systems by approximately 30% in 2027. It was also studying a further 30% increase for 2028.
The company is now investigating whether it can expand 2028 capacity beyond that level.
Customers including TSMC, Samsung and Intel require ASML’s machines to manufacture the advanced logic and memory chips used in AI accelerators, servers and high-bandwidth memory products. As Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and other chip designers receive more orders, foundries and memory producers must invest in additional manufacturing capacity.
ASML occupies a uniquely powerful position in this supply chain because it is the only commercial supplier of EUV lithography systems. These machines use extremely short-wavelength light to print the smallest circuit patterns required for advanced semiconductors.
That technological monopoly means there is no straightforward alternative if ASML cannot produce machines quickly enough.
Some customers have begun discussing orders for delivery in 2029 and even 2030.
Semiconductor manufacturers normally provide long-term capacity forecasts, but placing equipment orders three or four years in advance suggests unusually strong confidence in future demand.
ASML said discussions are moving beyond 2027, with substantial order activity emerging for 2028 and early interest extending into the following two years.
This level of visibility resembles the semiconductor shortages experienced during the pandemic, when manufacturers placed orders far in advance to secure limited production slots.
However, long-term order interest is not the same as guaranteed revenue. Customers could postpone or cancel spending if AI demand weakens, financing conditions deteriorate or chipmakers build too much capacity.
ASML must therefore decide how aggressively to expand without creating excess production capability after the current AI investment cycle eventually slows.
ASML increased the lower end of its full-year revenue outlook for the third time in 2026.
The company now expects annual net sales of €44 billion to €45 billion, compared with its previous forecast of €43 billion to €45 billion. Full-year gross margin is expected to be approximately 56%.
For the fourth quarter, ASML forecast:
The midpoint of the fourth-quarter revenue range is €14.7 billion, above the approximately €14.0 billion analysts had expected before the report.
If ASML reaches the midpoint, fourth-quarter revenue would rise more than 26% sequentially from the record third-quarter level.
ASML’s Nasdaq-listed shares closed approximately 3.8% lower at around $1,650, despite initially trading higher following the release. The stock moved between approximately $1,635 and $1,752 during the session.
Several factors contributed to the decline.
First, revenue narrowly missed Wall Street’s forecast even though earnings exceeded expectations. At a premium valuation, a small sales shortfall can outweigh a strong profit result.
Second, the wider semiconductor sector was under pressure after hotter-than-expected US inflation increased expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike. Higher yields tend to reduce the value investors assign to future technology earnings.
Third, investors questioned how quickly ASML can convert distant demand into actual revenue. Interest in placing orders for 2029 and 2030 is encouraging, but expanding production requires considerable investment and coordination across an exceptionally complex supply chain.
Finally, some of the quarterly profit beat came from the Mistral AI investment revaluation rather than ASML’s core operations.
Export controls remain one of the largest uncertainties surrounding ASML’s outlook.
The company cannot sell its most advanced EUV equipment to Chinese customers, while governments in the United States and Europe continue to consider tighter restrictions covering less advanced DUV systems and related services.
China remains an important market for ASML’s mature-node equipment. Additional limitations could affect sales even as demand from TSMC, Samsung, Intel and memory manufacturers increases.
ASML must also manage a geographically concentrated customer base. A change in the capital-spending plans of one major foundry could materially affect quarterly revenue because each advanced lithography system carries a very high price.
ASML repurchased approximately €4.1 billion of its own shares during the third quarter under its 2026–2028 buyback program.
The company also declared an interim dividend of €1.88 per ordinary share, payable on November 4. Cash and short-term investments increased to €12.74 billion from €7.58 billion at the end of the second quarter.
The stronger cash position gives ASML additional flexibility to expand capacity, invest in research and development, and continue returning capital to shareholders.
The earnings report reinforced ASML’s position as one of the most direct beneficiaries of the global AI infrastructure buildout.
Three indicators will be particularly important over the coming quarters:
Investors will also watch capital-spending guidance from TSMC, Samsung, Intel and major memory manufacturers. Their expansion plans will determine how quickly ASML’s long-term demand visibility converts into recognized revenue.
The third-quarter report showed that AI chip demand remains stronger than ASML’s production plans can currently accommodate. The stock’s decline reflected high expectations and near-term market pressure, rather than a deterioration in the company’s underlying order outlook.

The Dutch firm expects China to account for 20 per cent of its total sales this year, even as the US pushes for tighter export restrictions
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year, after seeing shipments to the market more than double during the previous quarter despite mounting US pressure for tighter export restrictions on less advanced chipmaking machinery.
The company’s sales to China surged 109 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to financial results released on Wednesday. That took China’s share of ASML’s machine sales to 23 per cent, up from 14 per cent in the second quarter.
The revenue jump comes as Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten faces pressure from Washington to tighten restrictions on sales of chipmaking machines to China.

articles.title: Terafab will reportedly receive its first ASML EUV tool in mid-2027 - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Terafab will reportedly receive its first ASML EUV tool in mid-2027  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk's Terafab will get its first EUV lithography tool in the middle of next year, reports Tim Culpan, citing sources with knowledge of the matter. But considering that the shell of the firm's development fab will not be completed until late 2027 and that tools will only begin to be moved in later that year, according to SemiAnalysis, the scanner will sit idle for some time.
Tesla broke ground on its research fab on the north campus of Giga Texas near Austin this past April. SemiAnalysis expects the building to be completed in 15 months and predicts it will take Tesla a further six months to install equipment and production tools, after which it will be able to start processing wafers, or rather experimenting with chip production to get the team prepared for completion of the Terafab volume fab phase 1.
Given how hard it is to get an ASML Twinscan NXE EUV lithography tool these days, storing it for several months before putting it to use may sound like an expensive slack period, but it's not the significant financial problem for Terafab that it would be for a traditional chipmaker.
The projected delivery of a conventional EUV lithography system to Terafab also indicates that while Elon Musk has praised free electron laser (FEL) light sources for lithography tools, the first-generation efforts of his semiconductor production company will rely on more traditional equipment. This is not particularly surprising, as Terafab is set to use Intel's 14A manufacturing technology. 14A will use not only existing Low-NA EUV scanners, but also next-generation High-NA EUV machines.
Using lithography systems with unconventional and largely untested light sources would require substantial modifications to the manufacturing process, extensive equipment qualification, and potentially changes to photomasks and photoresists, which would complicate the transfer of Intel’s 14A technology and delay Terafab's production ramp.
But usage of standard lithography equipment does not mean that Musk's company has no plans to use tools that are different from those used by Intel, though for now it is too early to make guesses about what Terafab engineers might change in terms of fab configuration.
SpaceX announced that it had selected Grimes County for Terafab in early August 2026. By now, there is evidence that work has progressed beyond clearing land, as drone footage published by Joe Tegtmeyer in mid-September showed foundation excavation and rebar cage installation at the northwestern part of the site. This suggests that contractors had begun structural construction by early September, although the precise purpose of the foundation is unknown.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Right now, SemiAnalysis reports that project Terafab Grimes phase 1 will be built in 20 months, equipped in 17 months, and ramped to volume in six months. Analysts project that the fab will begin operation in late 2029 and then ramped to volume by mid-2030.
An interesting note about Terafab's volume fab is that SpaceX reportedly ordered semiconductor manufacturing equipment in April 2026, several months before officially announcing the Grimes County location. This indicates that the company committed to its manufacturing plans well before the public groundbreaking. In addition, this makes the mid-2028 equipment installation forecast plausible, given the long lead times associated with advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Intel plans to begin risk production using its 14A (1.4nm-class) fabrication process in the second half of 2027 and initiate high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in the second half of 2028 if everything goes as planned. This puts Intel's ramp into HVM at least 1.5 years ahead of SpaceX’s Terafab Grimes Phase 1.
This means that while Terafab will get a proven advanced manufacturing technology, presumably with decent yields, it will not be the absolute best production node at the time, as TSMC intends to start volume production of chips using its A12 fabrication process in late 2029. A12 is a 1.2nm-class process with TSMC's second-generation nanosheet GAA transistors and backside power delivery. Intel will be close to unveiling its 14A-P node at the same time.
Nonetheless, since Terafab will likely exclusively serve SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI, a slightly less advanced node will not be a big problem for the company, as the potential cost increases incurred by using a more sophisticated manufacturing technology will be offset by using an in-house production facility.
