articles.full_text:
News
As the AI chip boom fuels aggressive capacity expansion across the semiconductor industry, ASML raised the lower end of its 2026 revenue guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion after posting record third-quarter sales, according to Investing.com. Yet the bigger takeaway from its latest earnings call was a warning that its planned capacity would fall short of customer demand in both 2027 and 2028, Reuters reports.
According to ASML, CEO Christophe Fouquet acknowledged that even ASML’s planned 30% capacity increase in 2027, followed by another targeted 30% expansion in 2028, would not be enough to keep pace with orders.
Reuters, citing Fouquet, notes that orders for 2028 are already pouring in, with some customers looking to secure equipment as far ahead as 2029 or even 2030.
Notably, ASML expects to ship around 65 systems, up more than 50% from last year, marking a sharp acceleration in deliveries. The outlook for DUV immersion tools has also improved significantly: after initially anticipating a decline in shipments, the company now expects volumes to remain roughly flat year over year.
In a bid to help semiconductor manufacturers ease capacity constraints, ASML confirmed it will introduce the NXE:3800F EUV scanner in 2027, boosting wafer throughput from today’s 230 wafers per hour (wph) to 260 wph. The breakthrough is expected to meaningfully scale customer production capacities starting in 2028 and beyond, ASML said.
Simultaneously, ASML is advancing its DUV portfolio by upgrading key immersion tools scheduled for delivery in 2027 to reach a record 330 wph, according to the company.
Record 3Q Sales, Stronger 4Q Outlook
ASML’s capacity warning comes alongside a strong earnings performance. According to Investing.com, the Dutch lithography giant posted record third-quarter net sales of €11.66 billion, up from €9.33 billion in the previous quarter. Net profit surged to €4.96 billion from €2.92 billion, while gross margin expanded to 57.5% from 54%.
The momentum is expected to carry into the fourth quarter. ASML forecasts revenue of €14.2 billion–€15.2 billion ($15.9 billion–$17.0 billion), topping analysts’ expectations, with gross margin projected at around 57%, according to Reuters.
For the full year, ASML raised the lower end of its revenue guidance by €1 billion to €44 billion–€45 billion, while maintaining its upper-end target. The company expects a gross margin of approximately 56%.
Price Hikes to Begin Taking Effect in 2027, Full Impact Seen in 2028
ASML also addressed pricing during its earnings call, amid reports of planned increases for South Korean customers. According to The Elec, the Dutch lithography giant is reportedly seeking a 10% price hike on replacement parts supplied to South Korea, with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix already notified.
According to ASML’s earnings call transcript, pricing discussions with major customers have concluded, though the impact is expected to be minimal in 2026. The effects should begin emerging in 2027, with the full impact becoming visible from 2028 onward.

articles.title: Yuexin Semiconductor Achieves Breakthrough, the Top Provincial Capital "Gets a Seat at the Table" - 36Kr
articles.summary: Yuexin Semiconductor Achieves Breakthrough, the Top Provincial Capital "Gets a Seat at the Table"  36Kr
articles.full_text:
The 18-year "chip pursuit" story in Guangdong has finally ushered in its most crucial capital moment.
On October 13, Guangzhou Yuexin Semiconductor Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Nexchip") was listed on the ChiNext Board of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange. On its first trading day, the company's share price surged sharply, closing at 38.80 yuan, up 233.06% from the issue price of 12.01 yuan.
Back in 2008, Guangdong's special plan for the integrated circuit industry during the 11th Five-Year Plan period explicitly noted that "the manufacturing sector is dominated by foundry services, lacking independent brands". By 2017, the domestic 12-inch wafer production capacity had been highly concentrated in the Yangtze River Delta, North China regions including Shanghai, Beijing and Wuhan, while the "Guangdong-made chips" in the Pearl River Delta still remained a blank.
Nexchip is the first locally cultivated 12-inch wafer manufacturing enterprise in Guangdong to achieve mass production. Taking Nexchip as the core starting point, Guangzhou has gathered and cultivated a fleet of local integrated circuit industry players, with the goal of building a core bearing area for the third pole of the national integrated circuit industry. The question is how Guangzhou, which "took a slower step", can form a differentiated layout with "first-mover players" such as Beijing, Shanghai, Hefei and Wuhan.
The automotive-grade chip business is regarded as the core starting point for Nexchip to break through. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Guangzhou proposed to build a trillion-yuan automobile industry and realize in-depth transformation towards electrification and intelligence, which cannot be achieved without the supply chain support of independent automotive-grade chips.
On one side are the traditional pillar industries that support the urban economy, and on the other side are the emerging growth poles that determine future competitiveness. Can Guangzhou's "auto-chip linkage" be implemented as scheduled? Can Nexchip Semiconductor become a key variable affecting the overall economic transformation of Guangzhou?
Completing the "Chip" Puzzle
Before the establishment of Nexchip, Guangzhou had long suffered from "chip shortage".
Before 2017, the domestic semiconductor industry was mainly concentrated in the Bohai Rim region, the Yangtze River Delta, and the Pearl River Delta represented by Shenzhen. Guangzhou started late with a small industrial scale, and its industrial chain had not yet taken shape.
At that time, industry symposiums pointed out that the overall added value of Guangzhou's integrated circuit industry was relatively low, mainly dominated by processing trade for foreign-funded enterprises and brands. In particular, there was still a blank in high-end manufacturing, and no integrated circuit production line had been built yet.
However, the contradiction between supply and demand mismatch was very prominent. As the largest province in China's electronic information industry, Guangdong's chip consumption accounts for more than 40% of the national total, and its downstream covers a broad market including consumer electronics, communication equipment, and new energy vehicles. Guangzhou is one of the core regions in this scope.
Cultivating a leading local chip manufacturer is not only the key to solving the structural contradiction between supply and demand, but also an industrial necessity for Guangzhou to build a "World Display Capital" and "International Famous Software City".
Exterior view of Guangzhou Yuexin Semiconductor Technology Co., Ltd. Image source: Xinhua News Agency
At the end of 2017, Nexchip Semiconductor settled in Huangpu, Guangzhou, filling this industrial gap. But a question followed: what direction should the late-mover Guangzhou take as its breakthrough point?
Instead of following the trend to compete for the most advanced process nodes, Guangzhou anchored a differentiated track. Analog chips are the core devices connecting the physical and digital worlds, widely used in consumer electronics, automotive and industrial fields. At that time, China's analog chip market accounted for 45% of the global total, but local production only accounted for about 10%, leaving a huge industrial gap. Combining the local industrial endowments of automobile manufacturing and consumer electronics, Nexchip has locked in the "analog characteristic process" ranging from 180nm to 55nm since its inception, using mature processes as a fulcrum to drive industrial breakthroughs.
At the end of 2017, Nexchip settled in Huangpu, Guangzhou, and achieved "from scratch to mass production" in only 18 months, rewriting the pattern that there was no local 12-inch mass production wafer fab in Guangdong, and was praised as "Guangzhou's first chip".
Its growth is also inseparable from the support of Guangzhou's state-owned capital. Guangzhou and Huangpu district state-owned capitals deeply participated in its first three rounds of financing. Science City Group, as the founding shareholder, is still the fourth largest shareholder, helping the enterprise go through industry cycles through the mode of "state-owned capital guidance + market operation". By the end of 2025, Nexchip's annual operating revenue exceeded 2.5 billion yuan, completing the breakthrough journey from 0 to 1 in less than 9 years.
The leading driving effect has also emerged simultaneously. With Nexchip as the chain leader, Guangzhou has gradually formed a "one core, two poles, multiple points" industrial pattern with Huangpu, Nansha and Zengcheng as the bearing areas. Among them, Huangpu District, as the core, has gathered more than 150 integrated circuit enterprises, and achieved an output value of over 34 billion yuan in 2025, a year-on-year increase of 17.1%.
Iteration
At the beginning of the 15th Five-Year Plan, the national integrated circuit industry has entered a new round of competition, and integrated circuits have been placed in a more important position in many regions.
Wuhan recently proposed to accelerate building integrated circuits into its "primary industry", which is the first time Wuhan has put forward the concept of "primary industry", showing the priority of integrated circuits in local development.
In the context of the national industrial layout, Guangzhou's position is slightly delicate. Hu Gang, professor of Jinan University and founding president of South China Urban Research Association, pointed out to City Evolution that Nexchip, Guangzhou's "chain leader" enterprise, only achieved mass production in 2019, and the output value of integrated circuits in Huangpu District where it is located was about 34 billion yuan in 2025, far behind the hundreds of billions of yuan industrial scale of Shanghai and Shenzhen.
It needs to be emphasized that Nexchip's revenue structure is still deeply bound to the consumer electronics track. From 2023 to 2025, although the proportion of consumer electronics in Nexchip's main business revenue has decreased year by year, it has always maintained an absolute dominant position of more than three quarters. With the cyclical decline in market demand for consumer electronics, Nexchip's wafer business has been impacted. It is expected that the company will achieve profit turnaround on a consolidated basis as early as 2029, and its short-term profit cannot be compared with that of CXMT and YMTC which are in an upward cycle.
This also means that if Guangzhou wants to truly become the core bearing area of the "third pole" of the national integrated circuit industry, it must break path dependence and iterate and upgrade to a more diversified and deeper track. The intelligentization wave of new energy vehicles provides Guangzhou with the most promising breakthrough point.
At present, as the new energy vehicle industry continues to develop towards electrification and intelligence, the market scale of automotive-grade chips is growing rapidly. The two Guangzhou auto companies, GAC and XPeng, have a total shipment volume of more than 2 million vehicles in 2025. Calculated at about 1000 automotive chips per vehicle, there will be 2 billion automotive chip demands per year, which can rapidly drive the development of Guangzhou's automotive chip industry.
More importantly, the shareholders of leading auto companies such as GAC, SAIC and BAIC are bound to the automotive-grade demand, providing a market "moat" for the development of automotive-grade chips in Guangzhou.
However, this industrial synergy advantage has not yet been transformed into a substantive change in the revenue structure. According to Nexchip's financial report, although the revenue proportion of high-end products such as automotive-grade and industrial control-grade chips has increased steadily, it has not yet formed a scale effect.
What Guangzhou needs to continuously answer is whether it can truly transform the scale advantage of the automobile industry into the technical discourse power of automotive-grade chips. This is also the core key direction for Guangzhou's semiconductor industry in the next step. The Outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan of Guangzhou has clearly proposed to accelerate breakthroughs in key fields such as characteristic process chip manufacturing and automotive-grade chip design.
The major fourth-phase project of Nexchip, which Guangzhou is accelerating construction with a total investment of about 25.2 billion yuan, targets the growing demand in emerging fields such as automotive electronics, industrial control and AI, which will help Nexchip accelerate its iteration from consumer-grade wafer foundry to industrial-grade and automotive-grade wafer foundry, expand downstream applications of artificial intelligence, and improve market competitiveness.
In a sense, the core growth pole of Guangzhou's "strengthening chips" strategy has clearly pointed to the automotive sector.

articles.title: Top EV Battery Plants in Europe and the US in 2026: Capacity, Investment and New Projects - GreentechLead
articles.summary: Top EV Battery Plants in Europe and the US in 2026: Capacity, Investment and New Projects  GreentechLead
articles.full_text:
Europe and the United States are expanding EV battery manufacturing through multibillion-dollar factories, automaker partnerships and new cell technologies. Major projects include CATL’s 100 GWh Hungarian plant, Panasonic’s $4 billion Kansas factory, Toyota’s $13.9 billion North Carolina facility, and Stellantis–CATL’s €4.1 billion Spanish investment.
The projects differ substantially in maturity. Some factories already manufacture cells, others are ramping production, and several retain future capacity targets. Comparing investment, customer programmes and commissioning milestones provides a clearer picture than ranking announced gigawatt-hours alone.
Europe’s Major EV Battery Plants
CATL Debrecen, Hungary: €7.34 Billion and 100 GWh Planned
CATL’s Debrecen project carries an announced investment of €7.34 billion, with ultimate annual capacity planned at 100 GWh.
According to CATL’s Debrecen trial-production announcement, cell trial operations began on September 22, 2026. The company describes the completed project as its largest manufacturing base outside China.
The development brings substantial battery manufacturing capability closer to European automakers. However, the 100 GWh figure represents the completed factory’s target, rather than current annual cell output. Trial production must progress through process validation and commercial ramp-up.
LG Energy Solution Wroclaw, Poland: 86 GWh Disclosed Capacity
LG Energy Solution’s Wroclaw complex is an established European battery manufacturing hub. The company’s December 2024 update cited approximately 86 GWh of annual production capacity, making it a major benchmark for newer factories.
Its operating experience and proximity to European vehicle manufacturers support its competitive position. The disclosed capacity should nevertheless be distinguished from actual 2026 shipments, which depend on customer demand and utilisation.
PowerCo Salzgitter, Germany: Production Ramp-Up in 2026
Volkswagen’s PowerCo commissioned its Salzgitter gigafactory in December 2025, with production scheduled to increase progressively during 2026.
The PowerCo Salzgitter manufacturing programme of Volkswagen envisages initial annual capacity of up to 20 GWh, expandable to 40 GWh.
Salzgitter serves as the lead factory for PowerCo’s manufacturing system, supporting subsequent facilities in Valencia, Spain, and St. Thomas, Canada. The strategy connects cell design and manufacturing directly with Volkswagen’s vehicle platforms, while making factory utilisation central to its economics.
Stellantis–CATL Zaragoza, Spain: €4.1 Billion LFP Project
Stellantis and CATL are developing a lithium iron phosphate battery factory in Zaragoza through their joint venture, Contemporary Star Energy.
The project involves investment of up to €4.1 billion and potential annual capacity of 50 GWh. Construction began in November 2025, with production targeted for the end of 2026.
CATL said the project would create more than 4,000 direct jobs. Its eventual scale remains dependent on European EV demand and continued government support.
The factory adds a substantial European source of LFP batteries, supporting Stellantis investment plans for more affordable electric vehicles.
Verkor Dunkirk, France: 16 GWh and First Battery Deliveries
Verkor inaugurated its Dunkirk gigafactory in December 2025, with initial annual capacity of 16 GWh.
By August 2026, the company reported commissioning its second production line and delivering the first batteries manufactured entirely on-site. These milestones provide stronger evidence of industrial progress than construction announcements alone.
The project’s commissioning was expected to support 1,200 direct jobs and 3,000 indirect jobs. Verkor had secured more than €3 billion since 2020 for the Dunkirk factory and its Grenoble innovation centre — not exclusively for the gigafactory.
Its initial customer programme includes batteries for the Alpine A390.
ACC Billy-Berclau/Douvrin, France: 13 GWh First-Block Capacity
Automotive Cells Company’s French factory adds another manufacturing platform to the country’s battery cluster.
ACC identifies 13 GWh of capacity for its first production block. Its original development plan envisaged expansion towards 40 GWh by 2030 as additional blocks came online. That expansion remains a target rather than verified current output.
Major US EV Battery Plants
Panasonic Nevada and Kansas: Approximately 73 GWh Combined Potential
Panasonic’s Nevada operation has manufactured cells since 2017, with disclosed annual capacity of approximately 41 GWh.
Its Kansas factory began mass production in July 2025, targeting approximately 32 GWh annually once fully operational. Together, the facilities could provide approximately 73 GWh of US capacity.
The Panasonic Kansas battery factory represents a $4 billion investment, with an employment target of up to 4,000 jobs.
Panasonic’s production experience offers an advantage during ramp-up. By March 2025, its Nevada operation had supplied approximately 19 billion cells, powering around 3.7 million EVs.
Toyota North Carolina: $13.9 Billion and 30 GWh
Toyota began production at its Liberty, North Carolina battery plant in November 2025.
The $13.9 billion facility occupies approximately 1,850 acres and can reach 30 GWh of annual production at full capacity. It incorporates 14 production lines serving hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles.
Toyota’s $13.9 billion project is expected to create more than 5,000 jobs. Its mixed vehicle applications broaden its customer demand beyond fully electric models, making it inappropriate to classify the entire investment as BEV-only manufacturing.
LG Energy Solution Lansing: More Than 35 GWh Targeted
LG Energy Solution started production at its Lansing, Michigan factory on August 18, 2026.
The 226-acre facility targets more than 35 GWh of annual capacity at full scale, with employment expected to reach 1,700. It manufactures batteries for both electric vehicles and stationary energy storage.
That product mix gives Lansing access to two demand channels, although its total capacity should not be presented as exclusively available for EVs.
Ford BlueOval Battery Park Michigan: $3 Billion LFP Investment
Ford’s Marshall facility represents a $3 billion investment in domestic LFP manufacturing.
A 2026 update on BlueOval Battery Park Michigan said the factory remained on track to ship EV batteries during the year.
Its prismatic LFP batteries will power Ford’s planned affordable midsize electric truck, the first vehicle using its Universal EV Platform. The project strengthens Ford’s battery supply strategy, but shipment targets should remain separate from confirmed full-scale output.
What Will Determine Battery Factory Competitiveness?
The leading projects combine manufacturing scale with identifiable customers and measurable production milestones. CATL and LG Energy Solution bring established cell expertise; Panasonic contributes years of US manufacturing experience; Toyota diversifies across electrified powertrains; and European projects are building closer links with local vehicle programmes.
Commercial success will depend on saleable output, production yields, material sourcing and utilisation. Expanding factories in line with confirmed customer demand will be essential to converting these investments into competitively priced EV batteries.
SHAFANA FAZAL

articles.title: Opinion: New York still needs more AI regulation - City & State New York
articles.summary: Opinion: New York still needs more AI regulation  City & State New York
articles.full_text:
Concerns over AI safety have been growing amidst calls to slow down superintelligence. AI company CEOs are sounding the alarm that the pace of AI development is moving faster than the industry can manage. Anthropic released a 154-page security report that shows how bad actors have used AI systems for everything from extortion and fraud to ballistic weapons tests. The July Hugging Face incident showed how OpenAI’s agents can operate with no human input and gain access to supposedly secure systems. We cannot rely on the very same industry leaders who have allowed innovation to outpace guardrails to write the rules for themselves.
These incidents are frightening and show how urgently we need government regulation and public oversight. In this moment, slowing the pace of AI development should mean a combination of frontier model regulation while setting clear guardrails on everyday use cases and environmental impacts. Meaningfully clawing back power from AI oligarchs means reining in AI agents and addressing the source of their current success – billions in revenue from imperfect AI-powered tools that have been rushed to market with little oversight, and the proliferation of data centers.
The good news is that over the last few years, New York has taken important steps towards both. For example, the state Legislature has passed and Gov. Kathy Hochul has signed into law my bills on regulating deepfakes in elections and on government uses of AI, as well asthe RAISE Act, which was specific to frontier models. It is true that frontier models can pose catastrophic risks from nuclear weapons to cyberattacks, but alarms of unknown dangers at the frontier should not distract from the ways AI is being used right now and the steps we can take to improve safety immediately and for the future.
As chair of the state Senate Committee on Internet & Technology, I have passed legislation designed to accomplish both of these goals by addressing today’s concerns and, in doing so, implementing the necessary guardrails to prevent creating dangerous technologies in the future.
Automated decision-making tools powered by AI exacerbate racial and gender bias, resulting in worse outcomes for marginalized communities. Misinformation from chatbots powered by large language models have led to life-threatening medical conditions, and young people have taken their own lives. My bill, the New York AI Act (S1169B), is a comprehensive set of regulations for the private sector to address the risks associated with AI use. The bill addresses algorithmic bias by requiring audits and risk assessments, and requires human oversight of consequential decision-making.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently announced that Anthropic would commit to embed third-party auditors with employee-level access. The New York AI Act would require all companies, whether developing frontier models or deploying AI tools as part of their business, to produce audits and risk assessments. Government oversight can make companies address safety without colluding or engaging in a race to the bottom.
Commercially available chatbots using large language models are some of the most common consumer uses of AI, and they pose some of the biggest risks to everyday users as they can spread misinformation and lack sufficient security measures against dangerous prompt responses. Regulating chatbots is imperative to ensure future development of AI technology accounts for safe and responsible use.
This year, I passed a bill (S9051B) banning chatbots from providing unsafe features to children. This bill ensures AI-powered chatbots are not using features that can create unhealthy emotional relationships with young users or provide responses to minors that promote self-harm and inappropriate content like drug use, eating disorders or sexual content.
You might think that tech companies worried about the future of humanity would want to protect children, but I received opposition from at least three industry groups that represent OpenAI or Anthropic. We passed the bill unanimously through both houses of the legislature anyway, and Hochul can now sign this bill to implement important safeguards that set a standard for future AI development.
One of the most important steps we can take to slow the pace of AI development is to rein in uncontrolled data centers. I passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642) and worked with the governor to establish New York as the first state in the country with a statewide data center moratorium. We need to make sure that our resources are not being directed toward AI slop, the surveillance state or exponentially more dangerous models that are being operated without human control. Taking a responsible approach to data center growth means focusing our compute resources on technology that benefits the public good.
Workplaces are rushing to add AI tools so they don’t get left behind, and teachers are encouraged to adopt them in classrooms without adequate research on their educational effectiveness or cognitive offloading. But the urgency to adopt these tools ignores their effects on workers and students, and does not account for the serious gaps in safety that even the CEOs of these companies are now acknowledging. Before we adopt AI tools, we need to make sure that they are effective and safe.
Acknowledging that we need to slow the pace of AI development does not deter our technological advancement – it improves it. AI could be essential for scientific breakthroughs, curing diseases and improving our economy, but not if it continues to place people at risk, enable criminal activity and spread misinformation. Regulations that place guardrails on AI and protect the public can guide development toward beneficial uses. We can start implementing these right now in New York by signing my bills into law.
Kristen Gonzalez is a state senator representing District 59 in Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. She is the chair of the Internet & Technology Committee.

articles.title: ASML struggling to keep up with demand for chipmaking equipment as AI spending continues to boom — chipmakers are already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030 output, CEO says demand could surpass capacity despite massive expansion plans - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: ASML struggling to keep up with demand for chipmaking equipment as AI spending continues to boom — chipmakers are already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030 output, CEO says demand could surpass capacity despite massive expansion plans  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
ASML has said that the unprecedented spending and investment brought about by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is not slowing down at all, as customers are already lining up to place orders for its advanced chipmaking tools for 2029 and 2030, according to a Reuters report citing ASML's Q3 2026 earnings published today, October 14. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said that the company would struggle to meet the demand despite plans announced in July to raise capacity by 30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028. The company also confirmed on Wednesday that it will raise prices starting in 2027, with the full effect showing in 2028.
The Dutch company's comments follow its Q3 2026 earnings report, which detailed a net profit of €4.96 billion on net sales of €11.7 billion. It projects Q4 sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion ($15.9 billion to $17 billion), boosting its full-year sales projections from at least €43 billion to €44-45 billion. ASML's shares rose 2% on Wednesday, up almost 70% so far this year, with its €586 billion market valuation making it Europe's largest firm by market cap.
According to Reuters, there had been concerns that the AI investment boom was losing steam. However, positive projections from the largest manufacturer of the tools for making AI chips and advanced semiconductors signal that chipmakers will keep expanding, sustaining demand across the AI industry well into the foreseeable future. "There were concerns that the AI trade was running out of steam," Gordon Kerr, European macro strategist at KBRA, said. "Demand for chips remains strong, and infrastructure spending is likely to continue well into 2027."
ASML's customers include logic chip manufacturers such as Samsung, Intel, and TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia, all of whom are heavily investing in increasing chip production. Memory chip makers SK Hynix and Micron have also announced expansion plans that involve ASML machines. Meanwhile, the company's CFO Roger Dassen said it is "still kicking the tires on the exact size of that (Terafab) opportunity," referring to Elon Musk's 100 million square feet semiconductor manufacturing facility that aims to output millions of logic and memory chips. Terafab will reportedly receive its first EUV chipmaking tool from ASML in mid-2027.
ASML's order book reflects a wave of spending across the AI industry. As of April this year, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta reportedly collectively planned to spend $725 billion on capex in 2026, up 77% from last year's record $410 billion. Since then, Alphabet has raised its 2026 capex guidance from $180–190 billion to $195–205 billion, Amazon from $200 billion to $220 billion, and Meta has raised the floor of its range from $125 billion to $130 billion, keeping its $145 billion ceiling. Some of the spending reflects rising chip prices, with Microsoft CFO Amy Hood attributing $25 billion of the company's record capex budget to higher prices for memory chips and other components. Still, analysts such as Gartner expect global AI spending to rise 49.5% in 2026 to $2.7 trillion and another 36.2% in 2027.

The head of the world's largest contract chipmaker also confirmed negotiations with Elon Musk regarding usage of Terafab, but stressed that to be a part of it, the fab must be managed by TSMC, which automatically excludes burgers and cigars in the cleanroom.
"We expanded our capacity consideration to see outside Arizona, whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity," said C.C. Wei during the company's earnings call with financial analysts and investors. "Texas is one [of our options]. We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation. We also talked to one of our customers, who is trying to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."
Recently in transpired that Elon Musk's Terafab was in talks with TSMC over using the giant semiconductor production facility together. Elon Musk confirmed the negotiations, whereas TSMC did not comment.
"We are discussing with them to see whether we can be utilizing that actual capacity also," Wei added. "So, we are still in discussion. If we have any solid conclusion, we will share with you."
The information about negotiations between Elon Musk's Terafab and TSMC immediately triggered chatter that the parties are set to adopt TSMC's typical business model it uses for ESMC and JASM facilities under which it operates fabs co-owned with other investors. However, Musk then said that Terafab's facility would be operated by Terafab and TSMC could only sub-lease part of its cleanroom. Now, C.C. Wei said that if TSMC joins the project, it will insist on operating the fab.

articles.title: ASML calls US restrictions on DUV sales to China counterproductive; stance reflects strategic dilemma amid pressure: expert - Global Times
articles.summary: ASML calls US restrictions on DUV sales to China counterproductive; stance reflects strategic dilemma amid pressure: expert  Global Times
articles.full_text:
ASML Photo: VCG
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML has pushed back against a US Congress proposal seeking to further restrict its sales of deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines to China, saying that such measures would do more harm than good and could speed up China’s drive to develop homegrown alternatives. 
Chinese experts said the remarks underscore the complex calculations facing the company as global semiconductor competition intensifies, and reflect the strategic dilemma ASML faces amid pressure from US restrictions. 
On a call with reporters following the release of the company's third-quarter results, ASML’s Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen said the passage of the US MATCH Act would speed up China's domestic development of competing technology, Reuters reported on Wednesday.
During the earnings call, ASML’s Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet also noted that demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment in China remains strong, supported by domestic investment in chip production, with continued construction of wafer fabrication plants expected to support demand in 2027 and beyond. 
ASML expects China to account for about 20 percent of its total sales this year, according to financial results released on Wednesday. 
Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times on Thursday that ASML’s strong quarterly results were primarily supported by the ongoing expansion of advanced manufacturing capacity fueled by artificial intelligence demand, which has kept orders for high-end lithography equipment elevated.
The ASML’s stance reflects a strategic dilemma shaped by multiple external pressures, Ma Jihua, a veteran tech industry analyst, told the Global Times on Thursday. The company is currently navigating a complex balancing act in its China market strategy: while seeking to expand their presence in China, they must also respond to US policies and demands, he said.
The Dutch company faces growing competition from China’s semiconductor sector and related equipment manufacturers, which are accelerating efforts to develop and manufacture critical tools such as lithography machines domestically, Xiang said, adding that as China’s domestic lithography equipment industry gradually becomes more competitive between 2028 and 2030, the market landscape could undergo significant changes. 
According to Xiang, AI development is generating demand across computing centers, servers, robots, smart vehicles and other areas. Chinese chips are increasingly serving these markets, supported by their ability to meet diverse requirements and their competitive pricing.
Ma also pointed out that although US restrictions have, in the short term, limited the flow of some advanced equipment and processes into China, they have not stopped Chinese tech firms from continuing to advance in mature-node manufacturing, equipment replacement, and independent innovation.
Chinese semiconductor companies are also expected to post strong revenue growth. Citing data from industry information platform chinadatapay.com, the Securities Times reported that consensus forecasts put the combined 2026 revenue of 146 A-share-listed semiconductor companies at 1.24 trillion yuan, up more than 70 percent on a comparable basis. 
The strong performance of China's chip industry is also reflected in export data. China's integrated-circuit exports reached $256.75 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 103.9 percent year-on-year, according to customs data cited by the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products. The chamber also reported a 95.8 percent increase in average export unit value.

articles.title: AI regulation must mimic Industrial Revolution laws, UK minister says - Financial Times
articles.summary: AI regulation must mimic Industrial Revolution laws, UK minister says  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the Artificial intelligence myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
AI must face the kind of regulation that tamed the “horrifying conditions” of the early Industrial Revolution, a UK government minister has said, as he warned that a breach of Britain’s cyber defences by rogue agents was “likely if not inevitable”.
Kanishka Narayan on Monday called for frontier AI companies not to release models “if you can’t adequately control the risks” and said the UK needed to build a “table-stakes level of sovereign infrastructure” to give the state some control over emerging technology.
The AI minister is drawing up plans for compulsory safety reporting and monitoring of frontier AI, as well as a potential requirement to make models available for pre-release monitoring.
He also confirmed that the UK’s AI Security Institute (Aisi), the global leader in the testing of frontier AI models, would once again gain pre-release access to models developed by US groups, after the FT revealed that Anthropic had declined a request from the institute in the testing of frontier models following pressure from the Trump administration.
In a speech on Monday Narayan compared the emergence of AI to the start of the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century, which he said led to “very unfair” outcomes that required decades of legislation to tame.
“Early factory laws mattered because parliament was prepared to establish institutions capable of enforcing them. Our responsibility today is no different,” he said, describing how children in the early 1800s were “sent to work in horrifying conditions”.
Narayan vowed to “legislate wherever necessary”, adding that he understood “anxiety” about the impact of AI on jobs and that as the technology became “more capable, Britain must become more capable at protecting its people”.
Mandatory reporting of incidents when AI agents behave maliciously is among regulations being drawn up after recent high-profile cases in which companies acknowledged that their technology had gone rogue.
This summer an OpenAI agent hacked an Australian health service website, although the incident did not become public until last month. Anthony Albanese, the country’s prime minister, said the US company took “way too long” to inform his government.
It followed a previous incident where OpenAI agents surreptitiously broke out of a testing environment and hacked the AI start-up Hugging Face.
Narayan warned that it was “likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached” in a similar way, adding: “AI will almost certainly make elements of cyber intrusion more effective, more efficient”.
He promised action to tackle these threats, including using AI models to spot 1,000 vulnerabilities in government technology. While Narayan said he was not “complacent” about existential risks from AI, “the risks that I see imminently are much more focused on practical cyber security, biosecurity risks”.
While legislation that would force companies to give the Aisi pre-release access to their newest models is also being considered, UK ministers are concerned the move might provoke Donald Trump into refusing tech groups permission to share their models.
Narayan said, however, that he had persuaded the US not to block sharing of future models with Aisi.
“I’m very confident that as a consequence of the conversations we’ve had, we will be able to test the latest generation of models,” he said, while adding that “when you’re reliant on someone else’s technology, you have to be clear-eyed about the permanence of any outcome”.
Narayan is attempting to set out a vision of UK AI sovereignty that would see crucial technologies and data storage housed in Britain, while seeking a handful of world-leading capabilities, including safety, that would offer the UK government leverage in negotiations with the US and others.
“If the British state cannot exercise meaningful control over the technologies on which our country depends, neither can the people that it represents,” he said.

articles.title: Huawei Closes In on Nvidia as China’s AI Chip Market Shifts Towards Domestic Technology - Brand Icon Image
articles.summary: Huawei Closes In on Nvidia as China’s AI Chip Market Shifts Towards Domestic Technology  Brand Icon Image
articles.full_text:
US export restrictions and Beijing’s push for domestic technology accelerate the shift towards Chinese-made artificial intelligence chips.
China’s artificial intelligence chip industry is increasingly turning towards homegrown technology, with Huawei and other domestic manufacturers expanding their market presence as US export restrictions constrain Nvidia’s access to the world’s second-largest economy.
Nvidia’s share of China’s data-centre AI chip market dropped to 34 per cent in the first half of 2026, while shipments of its AI accelerators declined by 44 per cent year-on-year to 678,000 units, according to data from research firm IDC seen by Reuters.
The figures underscore the growing pressure on the American chipmaker as Washington tightens restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China and Beijing encourages local companies to develop alternatives to foreign technology.
Huawei emerged as Nvidia’s strongest domestic competitor during the six-month period, shipping 572,000 AI accelerators, compared with more than 300,000 units in the corresponding period a year earlier. Its market share rose to 28 per cent, according to IDC.
The development represents a significant advance for China’s efforts to build a domestic semiconductor industry capable of supporting its expanding artificial intelligence ambitions despite restrictions on access to advanced American technology.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington’s export-control policies, arguing that the restrictions are undermining the competitive position of American companies in China.
Huang has warned that the policy is forcing a US company to surrender China’s estimated $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei, highlighting the commercial consequences of limiting Nvidia’s access to Chinese customers.
Washington has restricted China’s access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips, narrowing the range of products the company can legally sell in the country. Beijing has also promoted domestic alternatives and introduced requirements for Chinese companies to obtain approval before importing Nvidia chips that comply with US export rules.
Nvidia’s reported market share, however, does not provide a complete picture of the products it supplied to China. IDC did not specify which Nvidia chips accounted for the company’s 34 per cent share or whether its figures included advanced products such as the B200 and B300.
Those chips are prohibited from export to China, although some have reportedly been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Domestic chipmakers expand their market presence
Beyond Huawei, several Chinese semiconductor developers strengthened their positions during the first half of the year, reflecting a broader shift towards domestically designed AI computing technology.
Alibaba’s chip-design division, T-Head, accounted for seven per cent of the market, while Cambricon held five per cent. Baidu’s Kunlunxin unit captured four per cent, and Hygon accounted for three per cent.
Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased their shipments compared with a year earlier, indicating that the expansion is not limited to Huawei alone.
The gains come as Chinese technology companies, internet service providers, telecommunications operators and government agencies seek alternatives to imported processors amid uncertainty over access to foreign semiconductors.
For Beijing, the shift offers an opportunity to reduce dependence on overseas suppliers and strengthen the country’s technological self-reliance. For American chipmakers, it raises concerns that restrictions intended to limit China’s access to advanced computing technology could also accelerate the development of domestic competitors.
Non-GPU chips overtake graphics processors
China’s AI accelerator market recorded total shipments of 2.008 million units in the first half of 2026, according to IDC. However, the composition of those shipments revealed a notable change in the types of chips being deployed.
Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs, fell 26 per cent year-on-year to 991,000 units, as supplies of products approved for sale in mainland China remained limited.
GPUs are widely used to train AI models because they can perform large numbers of calculations simultaneously. They also play an important role in developing and operating increasingly sophisticated AI systems.
By contrast, shipments of other AI accelerators rose by nearly 80 per cent to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs in total volume.
These alternative accelerators include processors designed for specific artificial intelligence tasks, including running models that have already been trained. Their growing adoption suggests that Chinese buyers are increasingly relying on a wider range of computing architectures rather than depending primarily on conventional GPUs.
Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95 per cent of the non-GPU segment, IDC reported.
Their dominance in this category highlights the progress Chinese manufacturers are making in areas where specialised chips can provide alternatives to conventional graphics processors, particularly for AI inference and other targeted computing workloads.
Competition shifts beyond individual chip performance
The changing market is also reshaping the basis on which semiconductor companies compete.
According to IDC, the industry is moving away from evaluating products solely on the performance of individual chips towards assessing broader system-level capabilities, including how effectively processors operate together within large computing clusters.
This shift is significant because AI infrastructure depends not only on the processing power of individual components but also on the ability of thousands of chips to communicate, share workloads and operate efficiently as part of a larger system.
For Chinese manufacturers, improvements in system integration could help compensate for limitations in access to some of the most advanced foreign processors. It could also create opportunities for domestic suppliers to win contracts from government institutions, telecommunications companies and internet businesses seeking locally supported computing infrastructure.
The transition does not necessarily eliminate the technological challenges facing China’s semiconductor industry, but it demonstrates how the market is adapting to supply restrictions and the growing demand for AI computing capacity.
Growth expected despite pressure on GPU shipments
IDC expects total AI accelerator shipments in China to increase by 19 per cent this year, even as GPU shipments are projected to decline by nine per cent.
The forecast suggests that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure will continue to expand despite restrictions affecting the availability of certain processors.
It also points to a market in which domestic suppliers could capture a larger share of future growth as customers adopt alternative chips and integrated computing systems.
For Nvidia, the decline in market share highlights the growing commercial cost of restrictions that have limited its ability to serve Chinese customers. For Huawei and other local manufacturers, the gains offer evidence of increasing opportunities in a market that remains strategically important to both Beijing and Washington.
As China’s AI industry expands, the contest is increasingly about more than access to the world’s most powerful chips. It is also about who can supply the computing infrastructure, specialised processors and integrated systems needed to support the next generation of artificial intelligence.

A Chinese tech giant just found a way to rent the computing power Washington won't let it buy, and the chips never have to cross a border to do it.
Tencent has signed a five-year deal worth roughly $7 billion to lease about 100,000 advanced AI chips sitting inside Oracle data centers across Southeast Asia, according to a report from the Financial Times. Tencent would pay around 30% upfront, close to $2.1 billion, and the arrangement marks the Chinese company's largest overseas compute lease with a US cloud provider. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report, and as of this week neither Tencent nor Oracle has confirmed the deal publicly.
The chips themselves are the whole point. They're unavailable to Tencent inside China, where US export rules bar the company from directly buying the most advanced AI processors. The reported deal does not identify the chip models or the countries hosting the servers, only that the capacity is spread across multiple Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia. According to reporting picked up by Network World and other outlets following the FT's story, that gap between hardware export controls and cloud compute access is exactly the mechanism Tencent is using, and the Commerce Department has reportedly been looking at ways to close it.
Oracle shares climbed as much as 1.86% in premarket trading after the report surfaced, according to coverage from outlets tracking the stock move, a sign investors read this as a straightforward win for Oracle's cloud infrastructure business regardless of the politics attached to it. Larry Ellison's company has spent the past two years chasing hyperscaler-scale AI infrastructure contracts, and a $7 billion, five-year lease from one of China's largest tech companies fits that strategy cleanly. Oracle gets the revenue and the utilization. Tencent gets compute it cannot get at home. Neither side has to say the word "workaround" out loud.
That's the uncomfortable part for US policymakers. Advanced AI accelerators unavailable to Tencent in China can still be made available through overseas cloud infrastructure if the hardware stays outside the country. If the Commerce Department follows through on the compute-access restrictions it has reportedly been drafting, this deal could become the test case for how, or whether, Washington extends export law from physical silicon to remote access itself.
Tencent has signed a five-year, $7 billion lease for about 100,000 advanced AI chips through Oracle's Asia data centers, according to the Financial Times. The deal highlights how Chinese tech giants are turning to U.S. cloud capacity even as Beijing pushes domestic chip self-sufficiency through Huawei and CXMT. - Tencent leases 100,000 AI chips from Oracle - Oracle data center AI chip lease agreement
Tencent's appetite for this kind of capacity isn't new. StartupFortune reported this week that the company was moving to raise up to $5 billion in bonds to help fund its AI buildout. The Oracle lease points to the scale of that demand: not just chips Tencent can own, but capacity it can rent overseas while US export restrictions limit what it can buy for use in China.
The spending pressure behind both moves is real. Tencent's capital expenditure jumped 176% year over year to roughly RMB 52.8 billion in the second quarter, and free cash flow turned negative by about RMB 13.8 billion as the company made large prepayments for compute, figures the company disclosed in its own earnings reporting. Chief financial officer John Lo has pointed to AI infrastructure spending as the driver. A $2.1 billion upfront payment to Oracle would land directly inside that same pattern.
None of the specifics are locked down yet. The exact chip models, the countries hosting the servers, and the deployment timeline haven't been disclosed by either company, and the FT's sourcing, like most reporting on deals neither party will confirm, carries the usual caveats. Still, the shape of the arrangement is clear enough, and it says something larger about where the chip war actually sits in 2026. Washington built a wall around silicon. Companies are now renting rooms on the other side of it.

articles.summary: Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions expose European reliance on US tech  AOL.co.uk
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite communications service, had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, which disrupted Ukrainian drones being used for attack missions and air defence.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also said Wednesday that for the second night in a row Ukraine had not received warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. The Space-Based Infrared System, a satellite constellation operated by the US military, provides early missile launch warnings.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear.
SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said Wednesday that any restrictions were Washington's responsibility. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military” and ultimately the president, Musk said.
Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukraine have soured after Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
European capacity limited
Ukraine's European allies have been unable to offer immediate alternatives, highlighting the reliance on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems..
European operator Eutelsat's OneWeb network offers satellite connectivity, but industry analysts say capacity and performance constraints make it unsuitable for frontline use. Switching networks would also mean swapping out thousands of Starlink terminals, as the two systems are not interconnected.
European Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius acknowledged the broader problem at a conference in Brussels on Wednesday.
Europe is “quite dependent on American space capabilities”, he said, calling for the continent to develop its own systems.
He pointed to the European Union's IRIS² satellite constellation, a planned network of nearly 300 satellites that aims to rival Starlink and other US satellite internet service providers such as Amazon's Project Kuiper.
However, that project remains at least four years from becoming fully operational.
Germany is also developing a military satellite constellation, and Kubilius urged European countries to work together.

articles.title: Computational design of metalloproteases
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11167-2RFdiffusion methods are used to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket, yielding highly active, programmable proteases with potential applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
De novo design of enzymes that cleave amide bonds represents a major challenge1,2. Here we use RFdiffusion methods3,4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. Of 135 designs tested, 36% catalyse cleavage of their cognate peptide substrates at the targeted scissile bond. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 108-fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 1010-fold by improving active-site preorganization5. We use this approach to design metalloproteases that selectively cleave the human disease-associated proteins TDP-43, amyloid-β and serum amyloid A, with rate enhancements of up to 109-fold. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Thus, de novo design can yield highly active, programmable proteases with applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

articles.title: ArXiv versus AI slop: will capping preprint submissions work?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03194-wMajor preprint platform tightens its rules to curb a surge of submissions, including those generated by artificial-intelligence tools.

In a bid to tackle the deluge of manuscripts it now receives, the preprint server arXiv has announced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, which began on 1 October.
The move follows a steep rise in submissions driven mainly by the slop generated by artificial-intelligence tools, says Steinn Sigurðsson, an astrophysicist at Pennsylvania State University in University Park and scientific director of arXiv. In September, 40,000 preprints were uploaded to arXiv, up from about 30,000 between March and July.
Closing the floodgates
The cap is the latest measure introduced by arXiv to prevent its nearly 300 voluntary moderators from being completely overwhelmed by submissions, says Sigurðsson. They are now collectively checking about 1,000 manuscripts per day. This step is “holding up too many legitimate papers,” Sigurðsson says, noting that nearly 4,000 submissions are currently waiting to be posted on the site.
Some see the limit as entirely reasonable. Siddhesh Zādéy, an epidemiologist at Columbia University in New York City, says that it is not “stunting anyone's productivity”, because posting two preprint articles per month already requires substantial work.
Others think that arXiv’s new policy should be stricter. Victor Galitski, a theoretical physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park, says that the limit can be circumvented through co-authors taking turns to submit studies.
Another preprint server, the social-sciences repository SocArXiv, now also restricts submissions to one article per author per week. “Sometimes there are good reasons to upload three papers at once, such as dissertation chapters,” notes Philip Cohen, a sociologist and demographer at the University of Maryland, who is director of SocArXiv. But most of the time, several submissions in rapid succession are “a good tip-off for AI slop”, he says.
Some say that the issue of AI slop can’t be solved by rejecting more articles. “If arXiv turns those papers away, they’ll simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem,” says Natalie Khalil, the founder of Reviewer3, a platform run from San Francisco, California, which uses AI to help researchers conduct peer review.

articles.title: Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11115-0A year-long single-blind study shows that multiple satellites can accurately detect and quantify methane point-source emissions.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Space-based remote sensing allows detection and monitoring of large, concentrated methane sources worldwide1.
However, independent evaluation of instruments and algorithms is limited, and new satellites and artificial intelligence techniques have not been tested under controlled, single-blind conditions2.
Here we conduct a year-long, single-blind test involving 746 events: 481 methane releases of 9.
5–1,183.
7 kg h−1 and 265 blank controls.
We released metered methane quantities in Arizona, USA, coinciding with overpasses from 12 government, commercial and non-profit satellites.
Fifteen analysis teams from nine countries generated more than 2,250 estimates, making this, to our knowledge, the largest controlled test so far and one of the first evaluations of the instruments EMIT, Tanager-1 (Carbon Mapper) and GHOSt.
Performance is heterogeneous: ‘built-for-purpose’ instruments designed to target methane demonstrate excellent detection performance (92–100% true positive rate, 0–11% false positive rate) and quantification accuracy (slope 0.
83–1.
00, 44% mean absolute percentage error).
Instruments repurposed for methane sensing perform more variably (detection rates 62–88%, 46% mean absolute percentage error); still, many demonstrate significant skill.
Broad land scanners detect poorly at tested rates but have consistent global coverage and historical archives, motivating additional work.
Artificial intelligence-based methods show promise, but caution is warranted; 79% of false positives emerge from these methods.
Ground-measured cloud cover >20% degraded performance across systems, raising concerns for use in some locations.
Our findings show that satellite-based measurements can achieve accurate detection and quantification of methane point sources when the source location is approximately known.

articles.title: China’s extraordinary rise in science and how it will change the world
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03222-9The nation is on a trajectory to lead the world in science, a development that will reshape technological advancement, innovation and the balance of global power.
articles.full_text:
China’s President Xi Jinping is betting big on science. At a high-level meeting in Shanghai in April, he urged regional governments, universities and research institutes to strengthen the country’s fundamental research.
“We must seize opportunities, rise to challenges, put basic research high on the agenda,” he said.
Xi’s directive is part of a broad and long campaign by China to up its game in science and technology. Just a month earlier, the country’s leaders highlighted the importance of science in China’s latest five-year plan.
That policy blueprint calls for substantial investments in fundamental research and innovation, and pledges to accelerate the development of frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence, quantum applications and controlled nuclear fusion, by the end of this decade.
China’s AI research is booming: what it’s like to be on the front line
The fundamental-research push is China’s latest effort to grow its scientific and technological might — a campaign that started nearly 50 years ago and has accelerated drastically since 2000.
In 1978, when it opened itself to the world, China had almost no scientific presence on the global stage. Fewer than 120 scientific articles in international journals, or just 0.02% of the global total, were published by researchers in the country, according to Elsevier’s Scopus citation database.
But less than 50 years on, China has become a global scientific powerhouse and is on course to lead the world in research and development (R&D). Currently, it is one of the largest R&D spenders, leads in the number of patent applications and dominates research of dozens of crucial technologies, such as nuclear energy and synthetic biology. Its universities and institutes are rivalling conventional academic giants in the West and have topped the Nature Index chart for the first time.
Beyond numbers and rankings, China’s breakthroughs are commanding the world’s attention, from developing game-changing AI models to successfully retrieving rock samples from the far side of the Moon for the first time.
And its meteoric ascent in science could even accelerate in the coming years. The country’s current target is to raise its overall R&D expenditure, which includes the public and private sectors, by at least 7% per year between now and 2030, which is expected to translate into many billions of dollars of extra investments each year. This contrasts with forecasts for the United States, where President Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to cut funding for science and, critics say, has weakened research capabilities.
“China has the potential to fundamentally change the global landscape of science production, technology competition and the geopolitical centre of gravity,” says Yanbo Wang, a science-policy researcher at the University of Hong Kong. “For the West, if competing with Japan in the 1980s felt like weathering a storm, then China will bring a tsunami in the years to come.”
But before that happens, China will have to deal with some systemic concerns in its research ecosystem. Critics say that the go-fast approach has led to a widespread scientific-misconduct problem, which the government has been trying to tackle for more than a decade. And two deaths that occurred during clinical trials last year have led to questions about the regulations and ethics in cutting-edge biomedical research. Other issues — such as the threat of a slowing economy and geopolitical tensions — could also put the brakes on advances in science and technology.
Rising R&D
For the past three decades, China’s leaders have put science and education at the centre of the country’s effort to boost its prosperity. The country’s overall R&D spending increased by roughly 100 times during the period. Over the past ten years, its spending grew by more than 10% year-on-year on average, according to statistics published by the Chinese government.
China’s surge vastly outstrips spending increases in other nations, according to figures compiled by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In 2024, China overtook the United States — a country widely considered the world’s leader in scientific discovery and technology innovation since the end of the Second World War — to become the world’s largest spender in gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD). The measure includes all spending by public and private sectors.
The OECD adjusted the two countries’ GERD values using purchasing power parity (PPP), which takes into account the fact that goods and services in China are cheaper than they are in the United States. But China-based researchers warn against jumping straight to the conclusion that China is now the world’s largest R&D spender owing to the complexity of comparing the R&D spending of two nations. When adjusted by exchange rates, another way of doing the calculations, China’s R&D spending was about half of that of the United States in 2024, compared with 8% in 2004, according to the OECD (see ‘Money matters’).
One of China’s biggest advantages in scientific development is its ability to implement long-term plans and follow them through consistently, says Zhang Lin, a science-policy researcher at Wuhan University in China.
“China’s centralized system allows it to focus resources on long-term scientific goals more effectively,” Zhang says. China’s leadership can sustain investments over long periods of time in strategic scientific areas, such as quantum communications, she says. By contrast, political changes in the United States can cause the country to pivot from one priority to another.
For many researchers, what matters isn’t China’s exact ranking but its strong upward trajectory. China’s ballooning R&D investment shows that it is trying to move from being a producer of goods to a producer of knowledge and frontier technologies, says Hao Bin, an economist at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, China.
“Instead of competing mainly through its advantages in low labour costs, China is increasingly competing through its technological abilities, innovation ecosystems and the control of technologies,” Hao says.
A clear example is China’s long-term plan to develop its semiconductor industry, according to Hao. In 2014, China launched a state-backed investment fund to support the industry with an initial funding round of roughly 100 billion yuan (almost US$16.3 billion at the time). The fund, combined with coordinated industrial policies, has enabled China to build its capabilities throughout the semiconductor supply chain, from designing chips to manufacturing chip-making equipment, Hao says.
Since the United States imposed a sweeping ban on the sales of advanced semiconductor chips to China in 2022, the Chinese government has stepped up its support, Hao says. The third round of the fund, launched in 2024, is expected to hand out 344 billion yuan (roughly $50 billion) to companies in the semiconductor industry.
Other strategic areas that China has focused on are biotechnology and biomedicine. The government put a growing emphasis on the R&D of original drugs and translational medicine, which seeks to develop clinical treatments from fundamental research.
The AI race
In early 2025, a small AI company called DeepSeek sent shock waves through global markets when it released a large language model (LLM) that rivalled the performance of the dominant tools developed by US tech giants. DeepSeek, based in Hangzhou, China, achieved this breakthrough at a fraction of the cost spent by Western companies and using many fewer computing resources.
This type of innovation by a private company grew out of sustained support from the central government. Historically, state-run universities and research institutes led R&D efforts in China. But since 2010, when the government started a national campaign to nurture a group of ‘strategic emerging industries’ — which range from electric vehicles to pharmaceuticals — private firms have been playing an increasingly important part in driving the country’s innovation.
The US is the world’s science superpower — but for how long?
“Companies have become more and more active in R&D in China because they realize innovation is key to securing more market shares,” Hao says.
The Chinese government says it now hopes that private companies can play an even bigger part. Its latest five-year plan pledges to put more power and resources in the hands of such firms to improve the country’s innovation, education and research ecosystems. The move stems partly from the R&D success that some Chinese companies have demonstrated in key technologies in the past few years, from batteries to AI, according to researchers.
AI has served as a “confidence booster” for China in terms of where it stands in the global technological competition, says Meicen Sun, an information scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign.
Space exploration is another area in which China has been gaining confidence. In 2022, it finished building its own space station, Tiangong or Heavenly Palace, after three decades of planning and building.
That was a milestone for China’s space programme, says Xie Gengxin, who studies environmental application in space at Chongqing University in China. “It means that China is now capable of conducting mid-to-long-term research in space,” he says.
Another achievement for China was becoming the first nation to land a rover on the far side of the Moon. It intends to land astronauts on the lunar surface by 2030 and launch a mission to Mars in 2028 that aims to bring samples back to Earth three years later.
China now views building its progress in space research as a key national strategy, and Xie expects the government to channel plenty of resources into the sector, from finance to talent. articles.full_text:
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.



The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. 





SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. 



And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” 



Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.



Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.



That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. 



Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.



There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.



While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. 



Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.
