This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



The US military’s race to make fake blood



In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.



Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield. 



The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.



Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer.



—Andrew Rosenblum



This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday, October 21!  



10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries



WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.



WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries.



In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges.



Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries.



—You Xiaoying



Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries. 



MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers



Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process.



Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins. 



The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results?



This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

One more thing







Is the Pentagon allowed to surveil Americans with AI?



The ongoing public feud between the Department of Defense and the AI company Anthropic has raised a deep and still unanswered question: Does the law actually allow the US government to conduct mass surveillance on Americans?



Surprisingly, the answer is not straightforward. More than a decade after Edward Snowden exposed the NSA’s collection of bulk metadata from the phones of Americans, the US is still navigating a gap between what ordinary people think and what the law allows. 



Today, the legal complexity has a new edge: AI is supercharging surveillance—and our laws haven’t caught up. Here’s how the Pentagon’s use of AI has exposed legal gray areas.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?



Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.



The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology.



Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems.



—Grace Huckins



This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here. 



10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power



Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.



Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places.



Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out.



—Eshan Raul

The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarketsTemperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. (BBC)+ The attack has sparked alarm about cyber threats to food security. (FT $)+ It joins a recent wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes. (CNBC)+ AI is exacerbating the threats. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Meta has launched a bunch of new AI modelsIt hopes the models, built for complex, multi-step tasks, will rival OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s.(BI)+ They scored well on tests of reasoning, writing, and coding. (NYT $)+ Mark Zuckerberg says they bring Meta to the “frontier” of AI. (FT $)+ And will soon power the Muse agent. (Verge)



3 Anthropic warns that AI models may soon self-replicate across devicesWithout even requiring access to data centers. (Reuters $)+ It says models could spread through smart TVs and appliances. (CNBC)+ We’re putting too much faith in AI saying no. (MIT Technology Review)



4 Police have a new AI tool that finds homes from interior photosIt can match single pictures to Airbnb and Zillow listings. (404 Media)+ Police-tech giant Flock is tightening its rules. (MIT Technology Review)



5 The world’s first utility-scale enhanced geothermal plant is onlineFervo Energy’s Utah facility will supply carbon-free electricity. (IEEE)+ AI is uncovering hidden geothermal resources. (MIT Technology Review)



6 Did drone strikes on Yandex data centres blitz Russian bots?Zelenskyy claims the attacks quietened Kremlin-funded social media accounts. (Euronews) + But troll farm experts aren’t convinced. (Verge)



7 NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a Mars driving recordIt’s covered 28 miles since landing in 2021. (Reuters $)+ The rover passed Opportunity after detouring to study ancient rocks. (NYT $)



8 Elon Musk has become the 2026 midterms’ biggest known donorHe gave $158 million to a Republican Senate super PAC. (AP News)



9 Anduril and Palantir founders have backed execution livestreamsPalmer Luckey and Joe Lonsdale support Pete Hegseth’s plan. (Mother Jones)



10 A spacecraft has traced how a mysterious solar switchback formedThe Solar Orbiter’s discovery could improve space weather forecasts. (Gizmodo)



Quote of the day



“Many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI.” 



—Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar tells CBS News that Silicon Valley’s “social delusion” has convinced researchers to smoke because they expect AI to cure cancer.



One more thing







A brain implant changed her life. Then it was removed against her will.



Sticking an electrode inside a person’s brain can do more than treat a disease. Take the case of Rita Leggett, an Australian woman whose experimental brain implant changed her sense of agency and self. She told researchers that she “became one” with her device.



She was devastated when, two years later, she was told she had to remove the implant because the company that made it had gone bust.Her case highlights the need for a new category of legal protection: neuro rights. Explore how they could be protected.



—Jessica Hamzelou

MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.



Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. 



These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.



“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.



There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.



What are the benefits of open models?



Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. 





Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. 



If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.



Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.



But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”



Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.



Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.



But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.



“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”



Are open models riskier than closed ones?



The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. 



So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.



There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.





Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands. 



But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).



In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life



Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. 



The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.



The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.



Dissect what the breakthrough means for organ transplantation.



—Jessica Hamzelou



How much more can nuclear power plants give?



In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that.



Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants.



Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. But just how much additional power can we count on?



Read the full story to find out.



—Casey Crownhart

BasiGo is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.

Its pay-as-you-drive business model helps make EVs more attainable for private bus operators, while the company provides leasing, maintenance, insurance and charging infrastructure.



The company has more than 150 electric buses on the road in Kenya and Rwanda, with a reservation list of 1,200 customers. Now it’s targeting another major source of pollution on the roads: trucks.

articles.title: Daily briefing: China’s extraordinary rise in science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03322-6Explore China’s efforts to grow its scientific and technological might. Plus, how butterflies trick the eye and what could be the oldest shipwreck ever found.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
China’s extraordinary rise in science
In less than 50 years, China has gone from having almost no scientific presence on the global stage to a scientific powerhouse that is on course to lead the world in research and development. But before that happens, China will have to deal with some systemic concerns: a widespread scientific misconduct problem, questions about regulations and ethics in cutting-edge biomedical research and an academic culture that researchers say makes it hard for individuals to pursue long-term, curiosity-based projects.
Inside China’s AI research boom
Artificial-intelligence graduates in China are increasingly choosing to stay instead of pursuing opportunities abroad, a move that could help the country catch up to the United States in AI research. China-based researchers now dominate global AI-related publications, and the rise of firms such as DeepSeek and MoonshotAI has proven the capability of Chinese AI models. Competition for jobs is fierce and the pressure to publish is intense. But if China can retain its top talent, it’s possible that it could become the world leader in AI by the end of the decade.
News
GLP-1s get a makeover for the brain
After huge successes with GLP-1 obesity drugs, several pharmaceutical companies are turning their efforts to developing similar drugs to treat brain disorders. For example, pharma giant Eli Lilly has presented early clinical trial results of a compound related to tirzepatide for treatment of alcohol use disorder. And biotech company Kariya Pharmaceuticals has done the same for a GLP-1-like compound for Parkinson’s disease. But it’s not clear how exactly GLP-1 drugs might curb addiction, and past attempts to treat Parkinson’s with GLP-1 have failed.
Shipwreck might be world’s oldest
Archaeologists say that amphorae and other artefacts discovered off the Mediterranean coast of Turkey are from the oldest shipwreck ever found. The team says that, on the basis of the pottery, the ship sailed during the Early Bronze Age, between 4,700 and 4,400 years ago. And the pots still had some goo inside. “I looked inside and nearly fainted,” says archaeologist Karin Sowada. “It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins.”
Reference: Journal of Maritime Archaeology paper & Journal of Maritime Archaeology paper
Image of the week
Photographer James Lewin used an infrared camera to render the harsh sunlight at a watering hole in Kenya into dreamy black and white. It won the ‘Animals in their Environment’ category of Wildlife Photographer of the Year, developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. (BBC | 10 min read) (James Lewin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
Features & opinion
Can we teach old songs to new birds?
Birds that are moved, or bred in captivity, for conservation reasons might not have the chance to learn from their elders. But research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs. For example, in Argentina, researchers taught rufous-collared sparrows (Zonotrichia capensis) songs from hand-drawn annotations made in the 1960s. Someday, songs recorded by hobbyist birders could help restore lost aural diversity, says physicist Gabriel Mindlin, who co-authored the sparrow study. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says.
Reference: Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena paper & Scientific Reports paper
Whistleblowers need better protections
Whistleblowers who report misconduct at universities need greater protections against retaliation, and any resulting investigations should be handled by independent experts, argues astrophysicist N. Wyn Evans. “Challenge the institution, and you might spend years paying the personal, professional and financial price,” writes Evans, who experienced just such a drawn-out saga at Cambridge University’s Institute of Astronomy.
Video: how butterflies trick the eye
The bright and intricate patterns on butterflies might serve to create visual illusions that baffle birds — making it easier for the insects to avoid capture. By analysing slow-motion videos of butterflies taking off, researchers found that the insects’ markings can create the appearance of movement in one direction, when in fact they’re going the other.

articles.title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11150-xLongitudinal genomic analyses in patients with astrocytoma or oligodendrioglioma suggest that these two types of tumour differ in the mechanisms by which they become resistant to treatment, with astrocytomas accumulating copy-number alterations and chromosomal instability markers but oligodendrogliomas acquiring new driver mutations.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas that most commonly arise in adults under the age of 50 and exhibit variable responses to treatment1,2,3.
To understand the genetic drivers of disease progression, here we used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to characterize longitudinally collected tumour specimens from 183 patients with IDH-mutant glioma.
Samples were collected through the Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium4.
Most primary surgery samples were classified as grade 2 on the basis of histology (73% for astrocytomas and 93% for oligodendrogliomas).
We validated known genomic markers of tumour progression, including hypermutation and homozygous deletion of CDKN2A or CDKN2B (hereafter, CDKN2A/B)5, and discovered genetic alterations that distinguish between the evolutionary trajectories of astrocytomas and those of oligodendrogliomas.
Mutations in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and NOTCH1 were newly acquired in recurrent oligodendrogliomas, regardless of treatment, and were associated with an increased tumour mutational burden.
In recurrent astrocytomas, however, again irrespective of treatment, acquired focal oncogene amplifications and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions were associated with an increase in chromosomal imbalances, which converged with markers of chromosomal instability such as chromothripsis and whole-genome doubling.
In both types of IDH-mutant glioma, we observed a convergence of acquired alterations, genome-wide changes and worse patient outcomes, suggesting that treatment-refractory clones were being selected.
Treatment with temozolomide was associated with the mutational signatures SBS11 and SBS119 in both tumour types, whereas the radiotherapy-associated ID8 signature increased in astrocytomas specifically.
We show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumour progression and treatment in distinct ways, suggesting that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas differ in their responses to treatment-induced DNA damage.

Main
Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas, named for gain-of-function mutations in the metabolic-enzyme genes IDH1 and IDH2, are the most common primary malignant brain tumours in adults under the age of 501,2.
The 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification for tumours of the central nervous system (CNS) stratifies IDH-mutant gliomas into two clinically and molecularly distinct types: (1) IDH-mutant oligodendrogliomas (WHO grades 2–3), characterized by the combined loss of chromosome arms 1p and 19q; and (2) IDH-mutant astrocytomas (WHO grades 2–4), which lack the 1p/19q codeletion6.
Oligodendrogliomas are also characterized by mutations in the TERT promoter, whereas astrocytomas instead prominently feature mutations in TP53 and ATRX7.
The primary treatment for patients with an IDH-mutant glioma combines surgical debulking, alkylating chemotherapy and ionizing radiation; less aggressive tumours (WHO grade 2) might be treated with just surgical debulking8.
Despite these therapies, virtually all IDH-mutant gliomas develop resistance to treatment, which results in tumour recurrence9.
Because IDH-mutant gliomas are usually diagnosed in young to middle-aged individuals2, the ubiquitous emergence of treatment resistance results in a disproportionate number of life years lost3.
Various molecular responses to treatment have been reported, including alkylating-agent-induced hypermutation10 and radiation-associated CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions11, but it is unknown whether treatment-associated molecular responses exist that are specific to the individual IDH-mutant glioma types.

The Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium4 seeks to advance researchers’ understanding of how gliomas respond to treatment through genomic characterization of glioma tumours over time12,13. Longitudinal profiling studies from the GLASS Consortium and others have shown that a subset of IDH-mutant gliomas treated with alkylating agents acquires a hypermutant genotype5; that gains of oncogenes such as MYC and PDGFRA are associated with shorter post-recurrence survival14; and that radiotherapy increases the frequency of the ID8 mutational signature and broad copy-number changes11,15,16. These mutational footprints suggest selection of pre-existing treatment-resistant subclones or direct DNA damage associated with the radiation and alkylating agents, providing a rationale for targeting the engaged biological networks17. Here, we comprehensively characterize the genomic responses to treatment of IDH-mutant gliomas by analysing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and whole-exome sequencing (WXS) longitudinal datasets from 183 patients with highly detailed clinical annotation included in the GLASS Data Resource4. Our findings show how treatment shapes driver-gene alterations, mutational signatures, chromosomal instability and tumour clonality, revealing the distinct evolutionary trajectories in IDH-mutant gliomas with and without 1p/19q codeletion.
Clinical characteristics and timelines
Tumour specimens and clinical annotation from patients diagnosed with an IDH-mutant glioma were contributed by 21 institutions from Australia, Brazil, China, France, Germany, Japan, Luxembourg, South Korea, the UK and the USA (Fig. 1a). Owing to the longitudinal nature of our study, patients had undergone at least two time-separated surgical procedures to acquire tumour tissue through debulking resections (92% of surgeries) or biopsies (8%). Longitudinal datasets were generated from 581 surgeries in 239 patients, with available clinical data for 231 patients (Fig. 1b). After applying rigorous quality filters, tumour samples from 183 patients (94 astrocytomas and 89 oligodendrogliomas) at two time points were retained for analyses, selecting the first and last available tumour sample in cases of multiples (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Molecular profiling was performed on 183 patients using WGS (39 astrocytomas and 56 oligodendrogliomas) and WXS (55 astrocytomas and 33 oligodendrogliomas). Across the cohort, 122 tumour pairs were obtained at diagnosis (Tx) and first recurrence (R1), and 61 tumour pairs were included with other surgery timing combinations: Tx–R2 (n = 20), Tx–R3 (n = 2), R1–R2 (n = 19), R1–R3 (n = 8), R1–R5 (n = 3), R2–R3 (n = 7), R2–R5 (n = 1) and R3–R4 (n = 1). Analyses reflecting results from all tumour pairs are referred to as initial-recurrence pairs (n = 183); analyses that include only primary–recurrent pairs (n = 144) are indicated accordingly.
The extensive clinical follow-up in the GLASS cohort was a strength of our study: a clinical annotation dataset was established by standardizing terminology across institutions, comprising 262 surgeries in 119 patients with astrocytoma and 292 surgeries in 112 patients with oligodendroglioma (Fig. 1b,c). In addition to patient demographics, tumour pathology (2021 WHO grade and histology), surgery details (resection versus biopsy), treatment regimens (chemotherapy, radiation therapy and other treatments) and treatment outcomes (surgical interval and overall survival) were obtained.
To assess potential inclusion biases, we compared the clinical characteristics of the GLASS cohort with those of two reference datasets: The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)7 and the Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States (CBTRUS)2. Patients from our cohort were diagnosed at a significantly younger age than were individuals with IDH-mutant glioma in TCGA (Wilcoxon test: P = 0.006 for astrocytomas, P T SBS97 signature, which has previously been associated with deficiencies in mismatch repair, was found only in astrocytomas, as were SBS37 and SBS101, which are signatures of unknown aetiology. By contrast, C>A transversions dominated the SBS107 signature, which was detected in oligodendrogliomas but not in astrocytomas. This signature shows similarity to the SBS4 tobacco smoking signature29, and previous SBS107 associations have been found in bladder, renal and liver carcinomas29,34. Signatures ID3, also associated with tobacco smoking, and ID23, related to aristolochic acid exposure35, were exclusively detected in subsets of astrocytomas. Smoking is not associated with an appreciably increased risk of IDH-mutant glioma, and exposure to aristolochic acid also results in increased fractions of SBS22a and SBS22b, which were not detected, suggesting that alternative mechanisms are able to generate SBS107, ID3 and ID23. ID5, reported to be a clock-like signature, was found in oligodendrogliomas but not in astrocytomas28.
In summary, we identified significant differences in mutational signatures between oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas, suggesting that a variety of mechanisms underlies the initiation, DNA damage-repair response and clonal selection processes of both glioma types.
Therapy-associated mutational signatures
Therapeutic bottlenecks drive the clonal selection of tumour cells that can repair treatment-induced DNA damage effectively, and their mutational signatures might represent the footprint of the associated DNA damage-repair mechanisms.
We evaluated the enrichment of mutational signatures after therapy relative to matched pre-treatment WGS samples.
The temozolomide-associated hypermutation signature SBS11 was detected in 7 out of 18 astrocytomas (39%) and in 12 out of 23 oligodendrogliomas (52%) that were treated with temozolomide before tumour recurrence (Fig.
4b).
SBS119 was detected in 8 out of 13 oligodendrogliomas and in 3 out of 12 astrocytomas that were temozolomide-treated and non-hypermutated (Fig.
4c).
SBS119 was previously observed in three patients with CNS tumours, and resembles a signature that was identified when induced pluripotent stem cells were treated with temozolomide in vitro29,36.

articles.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
articles.summary: Incident hitting 700 supermarkets exploited outdated devices exposed to the Internet.
articles.full_text:
Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it.
French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire.
The hacks that didn't have to happen
Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores.Read full article

Most planetary scientists will tell you the heyday of Venus exploration was more than a generation ago. That is about to change.
Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The first, known as the Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), is now scheduled for launch in December 2030, a year earlier than previously planned. DAVINCI will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through the atmosphere of Venus, returning the first direct images of the planet's surface since 1982. A second mission, Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS), will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit.

articles.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
articles.summary: AI design tools make proteins that break bonds that are stable for hundreds of years.
articles.full_text:
A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.
Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.
Cutting proteins
The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)Read full article

articles.title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
articles.summary: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like…
articles.full_text:
Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.  



In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off. 



As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed.  





Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer.



Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions. 



One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says. 




A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started.




That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals. 



KaloCyte techs use a device called a tangential flow filtration machineto process unencapsulated hemoglobin.MATT ROTH




After processing, the hemoglobin is concentrated and then freeze-dried to make it shelf-stable.MATT ROTH




With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has. 



Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage. Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says. After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”  







In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit. Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s. On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding. In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors. But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products. Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians. 



As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success. Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles. The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets. The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale.



Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic. Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane. For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible. Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage. It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict.





This problem became all too clear in the 1980s and 1990s, when fears that transfusions could transmit HIV sparked interest in a class of membrane-free delivery mechanisms called hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs). One, named HemAssist, consisted of hemoglobin subunits linked together to avoid the rapid-breakdown problem. When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom.
Honey bees (Apis mellifera) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee's stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. articles.summary: KDE celebrates 30 years with a new Plasma release, a farewell to X11, and a movie.
articles.full_text:
Marking the 30th anniversary of software developer KDE on October 14, the company released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer, and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments.
After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025.
The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system. Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl, a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations.Read full article

articles.title: Hegseth’s dubious low-T screening may flag up to 25 percent of the Army
articles.summary: Medical experts explicitly recommend against blanket screenings.
articles.full_text:
Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, despite the true prevalence of the condition likely being a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA.
The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will lead to a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations for military members. Those evaluations could result in inappropriate testing, inaccurate results and diagnoses, and overtreatment that could cause harm, including infertility. Medical experts, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association (AUA), have recommended against blanket screenings for these reasons. Still, the Pentagon has moved forward with the plans, releasing clinical guidance in September.
The JAMA study highlights the reasons why testosterone levels are not measured in men without symptoms—and also offers a glimpse of how many Army members could become ensnared in the clinically dubious screenings.Read full article

articles.title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
articles.summary: The incident is likely 1st confirmation of mercenary spyware delivered by targeted ads.
articles.full_text:
Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app.
The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.
A clear warning signal
“This investigation should … serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.”Read full article

articles.title: What did the Liberty Bell sound like? Science is on the case.
articles.summary: Researchers hunted for clues in modal analysis of 20th-century replica bell at Penn State Behrend.
articles.full_text:
The Liberty Bell, with its famous crack, hasn't been rung in 180 years, but that hasn't stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation's 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell's replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today.
Historians aren't sure exactly when the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn't work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that "the old Independence Bell ... now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb." Nobody has heard it ring since.
This wasn't the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together.Read full article

articles.title: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
articles.summary: Its effect on people remains an ongoing question.
articles.full_text:
One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don't react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain.
“Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min's team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect.
Microdroplet chemistry
Min's lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.”Read full article

Rocket Lab announced Wednesday that its Neutron launch vehicle won't fly until 2027, citing an issue discovered during manufacturing of the rocket's carbon composite structures.
The announcement was public confirmation of what nearly everyone inside Rocket Lab and the wider space industry already knew. The most recent official update from Rocket Lab in August suggested the company still held hope of delivering the first Neutron rocket to its launch pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, before the end of this year, a schedule that would have almost certainly pushed the first flight into 2027.
But Rocket Lab's statement Wednesday about Neutron's schedule suggests the company is still struggling with manufacturing the rocket's large booster stage. Neutron's reusable first stage is made of carbon composite structures, which offer low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance. articles.title: Rewilding could help vulnerable islands keep pace with rising seas
articles.summary: Seabirds, native plants, and healthy reefs can help atolls build as seas rise.
articles.full_text:
Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.
Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.
Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.Read full article
